-scale anisotropies of cosmic rays
with energies above 4 EeV measured using the Pierre Auger Observatory. For the
energy bins [4,8] EeV and $E\geq 8$ EeV, the most significant signal is a
dipolar modulation in right ascension at energies above 8 EeV, as previously
reported. In this paper we further scrutinize the highest-energy bin by
splitting it into three energy ranges. We find that the amplitude of the dipole
increases with energy above 4 EeV. The growth can be fitted with a power law
with index $\beta=0.79\pm 0.19$. The directions of the dipoles are consistent
with an extragalactic origin of these anisotropies at all the energies
considered. Additionally we have estimated the quadrupolar components of the
anisotropy: they are not statistically significant. We discuss the results in
the context of the predictions from different models for the distribution of
ultrahigh-energy sources and cosmic magnetic fields.
  Finally, we analyze the arrival direction distributions in different regions
of the sky and at different energies. We find that the distributions in the
Southern (PA $\geq$ 45$^\circ$) and Northern skies are significantly different
at all the energies considered, while there are no significant differences
between the distributions in the Eastern and Western skies at any energy. The
differences between the Southern and Northern skies are not statistically
significant when the sky is divided into 6 equal-area regions, at energies up
to 8 EeV, but they become significant when the energy considered is above 8
EeV. The patterns of anisotropy in the two solar anomalies (June and December)
are also visible in the high-energy data, but they are not statistically
significant. The anisotropy levels in the two solar anomalies are consistent
with being constant with energy between 4 EeV and 8 EeV.

  We propose a novel application of graph-based reinforcement learning to
resolve delayed returns in continuous episodic tasks. We consider a set of
agents that share a reward-generating graph and have different policy learning
rates to develop our resolution framework. We show that our framework can
effectively resolve delayed returns by exploiting different learning rates and
shorten the resolution time as the number of shared experiences increases.
Furthermore, our framework is compatible with any graph structure and can
adaptively change the graph connection based on the agents' policies. Most
notably, our agents can benefit from each other without requiring a common
policy update step, and beyond that, they can also benefit from being trained
with different learning rates without delaying returns. We perform extensive
simulations on grid worlds and athletic-like tasks to show that our resolution
framework can effectively resolve delayed returns and outperform state-of-the-
art resolution methods.

different learning rates without delaying returns. We perform extensive

-trial C-band 72Gbit/s optical on-off keying
(OOK) system over 18.8km dispersion-uncompensated submarine optical cable in
the South China Sea. Chromatic dispersion (CD) of 18.8km submarine optical
cable causes four spectral nulls on the 36GHz bandwidth of 72Gbit/s OOK signal,
which is the main obstacle for achieving an acceptable bit-error-rate (BER)
performance. Decision feedback equalizer (DFE) is effective to compensate for
the spectral nulls. However, DFE has a serious defect of burst-error
propagation when the burst errors emerge due to the unstable submarine
environment. Weighted DFE (WDFE) can be used to mitigate the burst-error
propagation, but it cannot fully compensate for the spectral nulls because only
a part of feedback symbols is directly decided. Fortunately, maximum likelihood
sequence estimation (MLSE) can be added after the WDFE to simultaneously
eliminate the resisting spectral distortions and implement optimal detection.
Compared to the joint DFE and MLSE algorithm, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm
can effectively suppress the burst-error propagation to obtain a maximum 2.9dB
improvement of $\boldsymbol{Q}$ factor and eliminate the phenomenon of BER
floor. In conclusion, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm can jointly compensate
for the spectral nulls to achieve a maximum 3.5dB improvement of $\boldsymbol{Q}$
factor and obtain a maximum 1.2dB improvement of launch power (LP) at a BER of
$10^{-3}$. Therefore, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm can be efficiently
adopted to 72Gbit/s OOK systems for enabling reliable submarine data
transmissions.

answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last

Four-valued logic in the context of data merging, and (d) we give a novel
solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to
that of table repairs.

2D-3D correspondences to the perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm, multiple
correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and its corresponding
neighborhood and ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally,
correspondences with higher confidence are selected to determine object pose.

framework outperforms several state-of-the-art methods.

after all.

variant of eigenvector centrality
for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints on node importance.
Specifically, we consider a multilayer network defined by multiple
edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with
each graph representing one layer of the network and no inter-layer edges. As
in the standard eigenvector centrality construction, the importance of each
node in a given layer is based on the weighted sum of the importance of
adjacent nodes in that same layer. Unlike standard eigenvector centrality, we
assume that the adjacency relationship and the importance of adjacent nodes may
be based on distinct layers. Importantly, this type of centrality constraint is
only partially supported by existing frameworks for multilayer eigenvector
centrality that use edges between nodes in different layers to capture
inter-layer dependencies. For our model, constrained, layer-specific
eigenvector centrality values are defined by a system of independent eigenvalue
problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, whose solution can be
efficiently realized using an interleaved power iteration algorithm.
Furthermore, our approach is fully transparent, intuitive, and flexible, as the
definition of eigenvector centrality on a multilayer network is now available
as a toolbox offering a range of interesting centrality measures without any
need for re-interpretation of the concept of eigenvector centrality. Our
approach is also statistically valid, consistent, and robust (to
heterogeneities/imbalance and edge sparsity) as demonstrated by extensive
mathematical analysis and insight gained from a set of carefully designed
experimental studies.
  Our approach offers a novel perspective on multilayer network centrality,
allows for the investigation of dependencies between different layers of a
network, and provides a more accurate representation of the structure of
multilayer systems. Finally, our work shows how the idea of constrained
eigenvector centrality can be used to provide relevant information on the
importance of nodes in networks of networks.

global symmetries that could be present and explore how they are avoided.
Crucial ingredients that arise in such effective field theories are generalized

topological terms quadratic in the gauge field strengths which break a large

further be broken by assuming the existence of some charged states. However, we

generalized Witten effect, which implies that the spectrum of charged states is
constituted by an infinitely populated lattice. We further show that such a
lattice is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation that

devices that are being used to study multi-phonon phenomena both theoretically

particularly useful due to their lower decoherence rates, because they do not

bundles. From this, we highlight two outstanding features: first, we are able
to create dark states excitations in the quantum dot without the usual external
magnetic field needed to do so; and second, in a dissipative scenario where the
acoustic cavity and the quantum dot present phonon and exciton decay rates,
we show that the information related to the $N$-exciton state is retained in
the acoustic cavity long after the quantum dot lost such information due to
decoherence. This latter result demonstrates the potential of multi-phonon
scenarios to realize quantum memory devices.

developing more complex quantum acoustic systems.

system identification and design
problems can be formulated as functional optimization problems with
differential equality and inequality constraints. Since these problems are
infinite-dimensional and often do not have a known analytical solution, one has
to resort to numerical methods to compute an approximate solution. This paper
uses a unifying notation to outline some of the techniques used in the
transcription step of simultaneous direct methods (which
discretize-then-optimize) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization
problems. We focus on collocation, integrated residual and Runge-Kutta schemes.
These transcription methods are then applied to a simulation case study to
answer a question that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic, namely: If there are
not enough ventilators, is it possible to ventilate more than one patient on a
single ventilator? The results suggest that it is possible, in principle, to
estimate individual patient parameters sufficiently accurately, using a
relatively small number of flow rate measurements, without needing to
disconnect a patient from the system or needing more than one flow rate sensor.
We also show that it is possible to ensure that two different patients can
indeed receive their desired tidal volume, by modifying the resistance
experienced by the air flow to each patient and controlling the ventilator
pressure.
  A supplemental technical report contains the technical details of the
ventilation simulation.

ophageal tumor in CT images is known
to be very challenging. This is due to the low contrast between the tumor and
adjacent tissues, the anatomical variation of the esophagus, as well as the
occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians
therefore usually exploit additional knowledge such as endoscopic findings,
clinical history, additional imaging modalities like PET scans. Achieving his
additional information is time-consuming, while the results are error-prone and
might lead to non-deterministic results. In this paper we aim to investigate if
and to what extent a simplified clinical workflow based on CT alone, allows one
to automatically segment the esophageal tumor with sufficient quality. For this
purpose, we present a fully automatic end-to-end esophageal tumor segmentation
method based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed network,
called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), leverages spatial and channel
attention gates in each dense block to selectively concentrate on determinant
feature maps and regions. Dilated convolutional layers are used to manage GPU
memory and increase the network receptive field. We collected a dataset of 792
scans from 288 distinct patients including varying anatomies with \mbox{air
pockets}, feeding tubes and proximal tumors. Repeatability and reproducibility
studies were conducted for three distinct CT scans per 120 distinct patients.
Our segmentation method was compared against deep learning and traditional
methodologies. It achieved a mean DICE of 0.873, 0.796 and 0.751 for
single, repeatability and reproducibility scenarios, respectively. Our
reproducibility DICE is the highest compared to the state-of-the-art deep
learning and traditional methodologies.
  From the clinical point of view, our algorithm achieved promising results
working directly on CT scans without any additional information. It has the
potential to be used in clinical practice to reduce the manual delineation
error. Our code is available at
https://github.com/hunghv88/DDAUnet.

located in complex reservoir formations. To effectively produce from such
reservoirs and reduce costs, optimized well placement in real-time
(geosteering) is crucial. Geosteering is usually assisted by an updated
formation evaluation obtained by well-log interpretation while drilling. A
reliable, computationally efficient, and robust workflow to interpret well logs
and capture uncertainties in real-time is necessary for this application. An
iterative ensemble-based method, namely the approximate Levenberg Marquardt
form of the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML) is integrated in
our formation evaluation workflow. We estimate model parameters, resistivity
and density in addition to boundary locations, and related uncertainties by
reducing the statistical misfit between the measurements from the well logging
tools and the theoretical measurements from the forward tool simulators. The
results of analyzing several synthetic cases with several types of logs
verified that the proposed method can give good estimate of model parameters.
  By comparing the CPU time, we conclude that the proposed method has at least
about 10--125 times lower computational time compare to a common statistical
method, such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo. In addition, the
ensemble-based method can run in parallel on multiple CPUs. Testing the method
on a case inspired from a real field also yielded accurate formation
evaluation. Thus, the proposed method has promising time-for-solution properties
for real-time well logging interpretation.
  Finally, in real-time geosteering applications, in addition to estimating
rock properties and boundaries, we need to estimate rock types as well to have
a better description of the rock formations. We need to incorporate the rock
type model and update its probability in our real-time geosteering workflow.
This will require re-defining how to incorporate the log analysis results into
the geosteering workflow. Moreover, we need to leverage the data acquired while
drilling such as gas detection while incorporating uncertainties due to lower
quality of the data or lower sensitivity of the tools. This requires re-
defining how to include the formation evaluation with uncertainties into the
geosteering algorithm.

one of core knowledge
extraction techniques, named entity recognition (NER) is widely used to extract
information from texts for downstream tasks. Nested NER is a branch of NER in
which the named entities (NEs) are nested with each other. However, most of the
previous studies on nested NER usually apply linear structure to model the
nested NEs which are actually accommodated in a hierarchical structure. Thus in
order to address this mismatch, this work models the full nested NEs in a
sentence as a holistic structure, then we propose a holistic structure parsing
algorithm to disclose the entire NEs once for all. Besides, there is no
research on applying corpus-level information to NER currently. To make up for
the loss of this information, we introduce Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI)
and other frequency features from corpus-aware statistics for even better
performance by holistic modeling from sentence-level to corpus-level.
Experiments show that our model yields promising results on widely-used
benchmarks which approach or even achieve state-of-the-art. Further empirical
studies show that our proposed corpus-aware features can substantially improve
NER domain adaptation, which demonstrates the surprising advantage of holistic
structure parsing that can be further leveraged to adapt across different
domains.
  We release our code at https://github.com/zwj0241/NestedNER.

crowdsourced, human-generated image descriptions. The best-performing system is
then determined using some measure of similarity to the reference data (BLEU,
Meteor, CIDER, etc). Thus, both the quality of the systems as well as the
quality of the evaluation depends on the quality of the descriptions. As
Section 2 will show, the quality of current image description datasets is
insufficient. I argue that there is a need for more detailed guidelines that
take into account the needs of visually impaired users, but also the
feasibility of generating suitable descriptions. With high-quality data,
evaluation of image description systems could use reference descriptions, but
we should also look for alternatives.
  In this paper, we propose a novel framework for evaluating image description
systems that does not rely on reference descriptions. According to this
framework, an image description system is evaluated by asking users to
identify which of a set of descriptions matches the experience they had while
seeing the image. With this framework, the quality of the evaluation does not
depend on the quality of the descriptions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this
new framework by showing how it can disambiguate state-of-the-art image
description systems that are otherwise indistinguishable according to a
standard evaluation framework.
  We also look at the advantages and disadvantages of using proxy tasks in
evaluation. A minimal definition of a proxy task is any task that is not the
final image understanding task but still uses visual input as input. A
non-minimal definition would be tasks that are closely related to the final
understanding task, such as object recognition. A problem with standard
image understanding datasets is that they are often evaluated on the final
task only, while a system which excels on a proxy task (e.g. object
recognition) does not necessarily excel on the final task. With our new
framework, a system which excels on a proxy task (object recognition) is shown
to also excel on the final task.
  Finally, a well-designed set of proxy tasks can also be used to study the
capabilities of image understanding systems. We demonstrate how a set of
object recognition tasks can be used to study the visual vocabulary of an
image understanding system.
  In conclusion, a well-designed set of proxy tasks can be used to evaluate
image understanding systems as well as provide insight into the capabilities
and failings of those systems.

main factors - individual characteristics (e.g., a person's information
literacy) and social media effects (e.g., algorithm-mediated information
diffusion) - and has overlooked a third one: the critical mass created by the
offline self-segregation of Americans into like-minded geographical regions
such as states (a phenomenon called "The Big Sort"). We hypothesized that this
latter factor matters for the online spreading of misinformation not least
because online interactions, despite having the potential of being global, end
up being localized: interaction probability is known to rapidly decay with
distance. Upon analysis of more than 8M Reddit comments containing news links
spanning four years, from January 2016 to December 2019, we found that Reddit
did not work as an "hype machine" for misinformation (as opposed to what
previous work reported for other platforms, circulation was not mainly caused
by platform-facilitated network effects) but worked as a supply-and-demand
system: misinformation news items scaled linearly with the number of users in
each state (with a scaling exponent beta=1, and a goodness of fit R2 = 0.95).
Furthermore, deviations from such a universal pattern were best explained by
state-level personality and cultural factors (R2 = {0.12, 0.39}), rather than
socioeconomic conditions (R2 = {0.006, 0.16}), as measured by the Gallup
Well-Being Index, the Cultural Values Survey, and the Pew Research Center's
Income, Net Worth, and Assets figures. Finally, interestingly, we found that
the geographical structure of misinformation - i.e., the distribution of
circulation across the 50 US states - was insensible to algorithm modifications
(changes in sorting order of news items did not lead to an appreciable
reduction of the deviation from the universal baseline) but highly sensitive to
human factors (increasing explicit warnings against misinformation led to a
strongly localized increase of circulation, with top states increasing their
circulation by more than 3 times, with a normalized increase delta = 223%),
in a way that could have been prevented by algorithmic filtering (e.g.,
leading to a localized decrease of circulation by more than 4 times, with a
normalized decrease delta = -71%), underlined the need or effective
information literacy training and the critical need for filtering false
information also in social media.

lower-dimensional than the equivalent extended formulations. Our computational
experiments demonstrate the potential advantages, especially in terms of solve
time and memory usage, of solving the natural formulations with Hypatia
compared to solving the extended formulations with either Hypatia or MOSEK 9.

as conic extensions, we can make it easier to model and solve a wide range of

In this paper, we consider the multi-agent extension of the Motivation Dynamics
framework and show how the framework can be extended to encode persistent
multi-agent rendezvous behaviors. We analytically characterize the bifurcation
properties of the resulting system, and numerically show that it exhibits
complex recurrent behavior suggestive of a strange attractor.
  We then take the next step towards developing a control law based on the
bifurcation properties of a single agent in Motivation Dynamics. We propose a
multi-agent system with a rendezvous control law inspired by the single-agent
framework, and show that it induces recurrent rendezvous behavior similar to
what we see in the uncontrolled multi-agent system. We numerically show that the
resulting system can recover from loss of communication, and exhibit complex
recurrent behavior suggestive of a strange attractor.
  Finally, we experimentally evaluate the multi-agent system using a dual-role
robotic platform. We show that it can successfully rendezvous while
dynamically changing roles in a persistent way, and observe recurrent behavior
in its trajectory suggestive of a robotic strange attractor.
  Throughout this work, we strive to provide intuitive explanations of the
multi-agent extension of the Motivation Dynamics framework, as well as its
connection to existing decentralized control strategies such as consensus
control. We hope to offer a comprehensive introduction to both students new to

damage centres in silicon provide a promising photon-spin interface due to
their narrow O-band optical transition near 1326 nm and long-lived electron and
nuclear spin lifetimes. To date, these defect centres have only been studied as
ensembles in bulk silicon. Here, we demonstrate the reliable creation of high
concentration T centre ensembles in the 220 nm device layer of
silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers by ion implantation and subsequent annealing.
We then develop a method that uses spin-dependent optical transitions to
benchmark the characteristic optical spectral diffusion within these T centre
ensembles. Using this new technique, we show that with minimal optimization to
the fabrication process high densities of implanted T centres localized
$\lesssim$100 nm from an interface display ~1 GHz characteristic levels of
total spectral diffusion.
  We use this result to evaluate the potential of such T centre ensembles for
the implementation of solid-state telecom photon sources with extremely narrow
spectral lines.
  We show that while the narrowness of the emission lines (<10 MHz) is fully
compatible with the high data rates of modern quantum key distribution systems,
the underlying process of spontaneous four-wave mixing that produces these
narrow lines is highly unstable and prone to switch between three possible
dynamic states. We then report two methods that can be used to stabilize the
dynamics of the T centre ensemble: laser power regulation and chemical tuning
of the substrate lattice.
  We show that the use of a resonant microcavity can further stabilize the
emission spectrum by enhancing the optical interaction between the T centre
ensemble and itself. We demonstrate that these approaches mark significant
progress towards the reliable development of solid-state telecom photon sources
based on T centre ensembles, and that the implementation of these sources within
quantum networks is likely to be of the greatest benefit when high-performance
photonic cavities are used.

T centre ensemble in terms of the location of the atomic energy levels,
non-radiative decay pathways and the resulting quantum interferences. We show
how these features give rise to two distinct dynamic regimes that are characterized
by whether a repulsive or attractive hyperfine interaction is present between
nuclear spins.

used radio waves to scan the body. It is a tomographic imaging technique,
principally used in the field of radiology. With the advantage of being a
painless diagnostic procedure, MRI allows medical personnel to illustrate clear
pictures of the anatomy and the physiological processes occurring in the body,
thus allowing early detection and treatment of diseases. These images, combined
with image processing techniques may be used in the detection of tumors,
difficult to identify with the naked eye. This digital assignment surveys the
different image processing techniques used in Automated Tumor Detection (ATD).
This assignment initiates the discussion with a comparison of traditional
techniques such as Morphological Tools (MT) and Region Growing Technique (RGT).
It continues with a comparison of Machine Learning (ML) based techniques such
as Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and
Random Forest (RF). It further highlights the advantages and disadvantages of
these techniques. This assignment proceeds with an examination of algorithm
design and evaluation of ATD using MT and RGT. It continues with the same for
ML based ATD using CNN, LSTM and RF. This assignment concludes with an
identification of the ML based ATD as being superior to the traditional MT and
RGT while highlighting areas for future improvement.

Range Sectoring, organizes sensors in different sectors based on their location

coordinated to transmit in specific periods of time to reduce the hidden
terminal problem. To evaluate these two mechanisms, a protocol called HBCP
(Hierarchical-Based Collection Protocol), that implements both mechanisms, has
been implemented in TinyOS 2.1, and evaluated in a testbed using TelosB motes.
The results show that the HBCP protocol is able to achieve a very high
reliability, especially in large networks and in scenarios with bottlenecks.
Moreover, it is also efficient, since it is able to achieve a very high data
rate of transmission per unit of energy spent. The main contribution of this
paper, however, is the clear demonstration, through a testbed evaluation and
numerous simulations, that the performance of any collection protocol design
must be evaluated not only in terms of data rate and energy consumption, but
also in terms of reliability and, more important, network coverage.

work is presented. In Section III, the bidirectional link quality estimation
mechanism is presented. In Section IV, the hierarchical range sectoring
mechanism is presented. In Section V, the HBCP protocol is presented. In
Section VI, the evaluation methodology and results are presented. Finally, in
Section VII, the final considerations are presented.

coordinated manner to eliminate the hidden terminal problem, that is, to
ensure that nodes that are not directly in communication do not transmit at the
same time. To address this challenge, collection protocols have been proposed
in the literature [2] - [5]. Thus, in this paper, a new protocol for wireless
sensor networks is presented.

paper, we group object detectors into 3 categories in terms of context use: no
context by cropping the input (RCNN), partial context by cropping the
featuremap (two-stage methods) and full context without any cropping
(single-stage methods). We systematically evaluate the effect of context for
each deep detector category. We create a fully controlled dataset for varying
context and investigate the context for deep detectors. We also evaluate
gradually removing the background context and the foreground object on MS COCO.
We demonstrate that single-stage and two-stage object detectors can and will
use the context by virtue of their large receptive field. Thus, choosing the
best object detector may depend on the application context.
  We provide a new perspective on object detector comparison beyond metric
performance. For a given image, we visualize the region that deep object
detectors use as context by masking the input outside this region and measuring
the decrease in detection performance on a control set of images. We find that
the context region can vary significantly, both along the image (until far
beyond the boundary of the object of interest) and along the object of interest
(itself can be split into distinct regions). Interestingly, the context
region along the image correlates well with the attention maps generated by a
state-of-the-art attention generating network.

look-around metric. The look-around metric subtractively measures the effect of
context by comparing the performance of each method with a baseline method
working on cropped input. We find that the look-around metric is highly
correlated with the receptive field of the detection method. Thus, a single
scale method may use more context than a multi-scale method on the COCO val
dataset. Conversely, a multi-scale method may use less context than a single
scale method on the Park et al. dataset.

use of object detectors, as it provides a clear and interpretable understanding
of the role of context by object detectors. It is a simple and robust metric

symplectic group $Sp_n(K)$, where the commutative field $K$ is of characteristic

invariants are first of all the class of the group itself, the rank of the group
and -- for the rank greater than 1 -- systems of non-negative integers. The
second paper investigates the maximally compact subgroups of the groups

to the monomial groups studied in the thesis by W.M. De Wied. The third paper

challenging problem. In this paper, we describe the design and implementation

development of desensitization techniques to overcome this immunological
challenge. Compared with compatible KT, patients undergoing incompatible KTs
are more likely to experience rejection, infection, malignancy, and graft loss.
We study the optimal acceptance of possibly incompatible kidneys for individual
end-stage kidney disease patients. To capture the effect of incompatibility, we
propose a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model that explicitly includes
compatibility as a state variable. The resulting higher-dimensional model makes
it more challenging to analyze, but under suitable conditions, we derive
structural properties including control limit-type optimal policies that are
easy to compute and implement. Numerical examples illustrate the behavior of
the optimal policy under different mismatch levels and highlight the importance
of explicitly incorporating the incompatibility level into the acceptance
decision when desensitization therapy is an option.

management of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) from its onset until death. The
goal is to maximize the expected quality of life (QOL) until death, subject to
a budget constraint for dialysis and possible kidney transplants. In addition,
we incorporate a state variable to capture the level of immunological
incompatibility between a patient and available donor kidneys, and consider
therapy that reduces this mismatch. Due to the tractable structure of the
resulting six-dimensional transition rate vector, we are able to derive
explicitly the optimal transition rates and QOL over time. From these, we can
directly compute the optimal action (e.g., accept/reject a kidney, start/stop
dialysis, undergo therapy) that maximizes QOL subject to the given budget. We
illustrate the effectiveness of the optimal policy via a set of realistic
scenarios representing patients with different disease histories and transplant
opportunities.

goal is to explain how embeddings, that are now widely used in NLP (Natural
Language Processing), are influenced by the distribution of terms in the
documents of the considered corpus. We use the Poisson distribution to model
this distribution and we show how the algorithm produces well known
properties, such as the limited vocabulary bias, as well as a particular
structural analysis of the underlying graph, revealed by an original
mathematical formulation of a game played between terms. Finally, we provide
intrinsic evaluation metrics, based on Riemannian metrics, to assess the
quality of the produced embeddings, and we illustrate their relevance on three
standard datasets. In particular we show how the quality of the embeddings
increases when the window parameter increases, which is, to our knowledge, a
new result validation of the word2vec approach.
  We provide a Python implementation of our algorithm, called
PoissonContext, which can be compared to the standard word2vec. We rigorously
proves that, when the window parameter $n$ increases, its implementation
produces embedding very similar to the ones produced by the standard word2vec
when $n=1$, thus illustrating a higher quality when $n>1$. We conduct an
extensive empirical evaluation on three standard text classification
datasets. Our selection of learning schemes and evaluation protocols aims at
illustrating the benefit of the PoissonContext approach on embeddings and
classification tasks. Empirical results show that increasing the window
parameter $n$ often leads to an improvement of the classification performance,
as long as $n$ is small. We illustrate that the default setting $n=1$ might be
too restrictive in many situations, and that setting $n=3$ often provides a
nice trade-off between embedding quality and classification performance.

compositional interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed
category of FVect and linear maps have been made, but in these proposals the
syntax-semantics mapping ignores the control modalities, effectively
restricting their role to the syntax. Our aim is to turn the modalities into
first-class citizens of the vectorial interpretation. Building on the
directional density matrix semantics, we extend the interpretation of the type
system with an extra spin density matrix space. The interpretation of proofs
then results in ambiguous derivations being tensored with orthogonal spin
states. Our method introduces a way of simultaneously representing co-existing
interpretations of ambiguous utterances, and provides a uniform framework for
the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity.
  We achieve this extension by means of a careful examination of the
connection between the syntax and the semantics. We show that the original
Lambek Calculus can be seen as a particular kind of controlled extension, and
that the original (uncontrolled) Lambek Calculus can be obtained from the
controlled extensions by means of a forgetful functor that forgets the
modality applied to proofs. We provide an explicit description of this
connection and show that its natural extension to the vectorial interpretation
introduces the extra spin density matrix space over the complex numbers.

  Many stochastic systems have multiple factors that impact the output
trajectories; e.g., the cartpole system has both wind and gravity. To enable
effective experience replay for such systems, we propose a multi-task based
variance reduction experience replay (MT-VRER) framework that can adaptively
balance the contribution of different factors during policy optimization. The
key idea is to treat different factors as separate tasks and mark the samples
with the same factor with respect to that task as their corresponding
counterparts in a single-task scenario. We empirically show that samples of the
same factor can be compressed to lower dimensional space where they can be
closer to each other, and the overall performance can be improved by a
state-of-the-art optimization approach enhanced with our proposed framework.
Experimental results on both discrete and continuous environments
demonstrate the effectiveness of MT-VRER.
  We propose a constrained based experience replay (CBER) framework that can
selectively reuse the samples that are preferred by the current target
distribution and avoided the interference of unnecessary samples. To selectively
reuse samples, we introduce a constraint to minimize the difference between the
empirical distribution of the current sample batch and the target distribution.

towards low $T$) in the thinnest, most magnetic samples. The origin of this
bipartite relaxation is discussed.

fluctuations associated with magnetic disorder (alloying effects) and/or
magnetic layer boundary phases. The origin of the large amplitude of this
component in thin LaNiO$_3$ films remains an open question, but may be related
to an enhancement of magnetic layer boundary effects in films where the
average distance between layers is large. The slow relaxing component is
assigned to bulk magnetic fluctuations in the magnetic layer, and its resistance
ratio indicates an enhanced mean carrier pocket size in these superlattices
compared to the bulk material.

electronics of d-electron metals and superconductors and set the stage for

propose a simple scoring algorithm, based on bipartite graph matching, to
optimally incorporate a set of diverse references. We study multiple language
generation tasks at different levels of predictive conversation depth, using
textual attributes induced automatically from pretrained classifiers. Our
culminating task is a challenging theory of mind problem, a controllable
generation task which requires reasoning about the expected reaction of the
listener.
  For branching factor 10, we find that simple baseline models which
independently generate each word in a conversation perform well compared to
state-of-the-art conversational models. To study the effect of prediction
depth, we examine tasks which require prediction of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 words
in the future. We find that performance increases consistently with prediction
depth, suggesting a lesson that models should be evaluated on tasks which
stretch their conversation capacity.
  Our analysis yields insights into the behavior of baseline and state-of-the-art
models, and we propose a set of data processing techniques that can improve
state-of-the-art generation performance by incorporating diverse references,
and improve theoretical task performance by filtering out unpleasant
alternatives. Overall, our data and methods provide a framework for studying
highly branching dialog which is less sensitive to overfitting, allowing for a
more comprehensive investigation of dialog generation models.

exact ergodic capacity (EC) of a
point-to-point multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system assisted by an
intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). In addition, we account for the effects
of correlated Rayleigh fading and the intertwinement between the amplitude and
the phase shift of the reflecting coefficient of each IRS element, which are
usually both neglected despite their presence in practice. Random matrix theory
tools allow to derive the probability density function (PDF) of the cascaded
channel in closed form, and subsequently, the EC, which depend only on the
large-scale statistics and the phase shifts. Notably, we optimize the EC with
respect to the phase shifts with low overhead, i.e., once per several coherence
intervals instead of the burden of frequent necessary optimization required by
expressions being dependent on instantaneous channel information. Monte-Carlo
(MC) simulations verify the analytical results and demonstrate the insightful
interplay among the key parameters and their impact on the EC.
  Besides, we extend the results to the case of a multiple-input single-output
(MISO) receiver. We show that for the special case of equal phase shifts and
isotropic receiver antennas, the EC for both the MIMO and MISO cases coincide.
Moreover, we optimize the reflecting coefficients for a given number of
scattered waves or iridescence using a low-overhead iterative algorithm. Numeric
results investigate the performance of the proposed scheme in various
scenarios compared to no-IRS and per-element optimization as benchmarks.
  Keywords: Intelligent reflecting surface, Iridescence, Correlated Rayleigh
fading, Exact ergodic capacity, MIMO, MISO.

popular MediaWiki platform that
makes a wiki into a powerful environment for collaborating on
publication-quality manuscripts and software projects. Developed in Jonathan
Dushoff's theoretical biology lab at McMaster University and available as free
software, it allows wiki users to work together on anything that can be done by
using UNIX commands to transform textual "source code" into output. Researchers
can use it to collaborate on programs written in R, python, C, or any other
language, and there are special features to support easy work on LaTeX
documents. It develops the potential of the wiki medium to serve as a
combination collaborative text editor, development environment, revision
control system, and publishing platform. Its potential uses are open-ended -
its processing is controlled by makefiles that are straightforward to customize
- and its modular design is intended to allow parts of it to be adapted to
other purposes.
  Developed to meet the needs of a research group, WorkingWiki is designed to
autonomously perform many tasks that would be done by a human researcher. It
tries to reflect an intuitive view of the "life cycle" of a research project,
from initial idea to final publication. It defines itself in terms of a
"top-level" LaTeX document that serves as a control center for the rest of the
document, which includes everything from all the sources that contribute to it
to everything needed to build and distribute it. Users work on this control
document by making changes to pieces of "source code" that are translated into
it; they can also add new sources and modify the makefiles that control the
transformation of all of its sources into output.

models result in dynamically-bound clusters at neighboring sites. We show that
the dynamics of these clusters in two-dimensional lattices is remarkably
different and richer than that of repulsively-bound on-site clusters in gases
without inter-site interactions. Whereas on-site pairs move in the same lattice
as individual particles, nearest-neighbor dimers perform an interacting quantum
walk in a different lattice geometry, leading to a peculiar dynamics
characterized by more than one time scale. The latter is general for any
lattice geometry, but it is especially relevant in triangular and diamond
lattices, where dimers move resonantly in an effective kagome and Lieb lattice,
respectively. As a result, dimers experience partial quasi-localization due to
an effective flat band, and may move slower than longer clusters. This
surprising link between anomalously slow quantum walk dynamics in these models
and flat-band physics may be readily observed in experiments with lanthanide
atoms.
  We also show that spin clusters in these models are characterized by
non-Abelian emergent symmetries, which lead to anomalous holonomy effects. For
a spin trimer in a one-dimensional XXZ spin model, this results in a peculiar
non-Abelian dynamics where the holonomy of one particle is literally "carried"
on the bond between neighboring dimers. This is manifested by a non-Abelian
effective rotation of the spin trimer, which is equivalent to a combination of
two SU(2) rotations, and cannot be reduced to simple successive rotations of
its constituent spin pairs. Moreover, we find that this holonomy is generally
preserved along its path, but it can be strictly prohibited in certain
scenarios. The latter may be utilized to design faithful measurements of the
spin trimer.
  Our findings uncover the rich physics of interacting clusters in two-dimensional
lattices, and demonstrate the outstanding link between flat-band physics and
fundamental dynamics in quantum many-body systems.

the law of gravity at the low accelerations typical of galactic outskirts. I
consider the feasibility of this wide binary test using the `line velocity'
method. This involves considering only the velocity components along the
direction within the sky plane orthogonal to the systemic proper motion of each
WB.
  I apply this technique to the WB sample of Hernandez et. al. (2019),
carefully accounting for large-angle effects at one order beyond leading. Based
on Monte Carlo trials, the uncertainty in the one-dimensional velocity
dispersion is $\approx 100$ m/s when using sky-projected relative velocities.
Using line velocities reduces this to $\approx 30$ m/s because these are much
less affected by distance uncertainties.
  My analysis does not support the Hernandez et. al. (2019) claim of a clear
departure from Newtonian dynamics beyond a radius of $\approx 10$ kAU, partly
because I use $2\sigma$ outlier rejection to clean their sample first.
Nonetheless, the uncertainties are small enough that existing WB data are
nearly sufficient to distinguish Newtonian dynamics from Modified Newtonian
Dynamics. I estimate that $\approx 1000$ WB systems will be required for this
purpose if using only line velocities.
  In addition to a larger sample, it will also be important to control for
systematics like undetected companions and stellar mass biases. A simpler
approach is to focus on the dynamics of WB centers (which are much more massive
than their wide separations) rather than the WBs themselves.
  Finally, I note that HBs (hyper-wide binaries) may be relevant for small
range tests of gravity at even lower accelerations.

learning (VFL). In HFL, participants share the same feature space and

real-world VFL frameworks. We design and implement two practical privacy
attacks: reverse multiplication attack for the logistic regression VFL
protocol; and reverse sum attack for the XGBoost VFL protocol. We empirically
show that the two attacks are (1) effective - the adversary can successfully
steal the private training data, even when the intermediate outputs are
encrypted to protect data privacy; (2) evasive - the attacks do not deviate

model; and (3) easy - the adversary needs little prior knowledge about the data
distribution of the target participant. We also show the leaked information is
as effective as the raw training data in training an alternative classifier. We
further discuss the practicality of the attacks by demonstrating the
performance of the attacks on larger-scale datasets and DNN protocols. We
finally highlight the necessity of secure protocol design for VFL and appeal
for further research in this area.

valve replacement
surgery in patients with the congenital heart disease Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
is mainly based on ventricular volume and function according to current
guidelines. Both of these two biomarkers are most reliably assessed by
segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. In several grand
challenges in the last years, U-Net architectures have shown impressive results
on the provided data. However, in clinical practice, data sets are more diverse
considering individual pathologies and image properties derived from different
scanner properties. Additionally, specific training data for complex rare
diseases like TOF is scarce.
  For this work, 1) we assessed the accuracy gap when using a publicly
available labelled data set (the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC)
data set) for training and subsequent applying it to CMR data of TOF patients
and vice versa and 2) whether we can achieve similar results when applying the
model to a more heterogeneous data base.
  Multiple deep learning models were trained with four-fold cross validation.
Afterwards they were evaluated on the respective unseen CMR images from the
other collection. Our results confirm that current deep learning models can
achieve excellent results (left ventricle dice of
$0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.007}$ train/validation) when sufficient labelled
data from the same population is available. However, when applying the model
to CMR images from TOF patients, the results degrade significantly (dice of
$0.823\pm{0.012}$/$0.767\pm{0.018}$ train/validation). Interestingly, a
pipeline consisting of first being trained and then evaluated on CMR images
from TOF patients yields comparable results (dice of $0.815\pm{0.010}$/$
0.758\pm{0.017}$ train/validation) to being trained and evaluated on CMR images
from the general available data set.
  We conclude that general available data sets should not be used for training
deep learning models for specific diseases like TOF. Instead, one should
attempt to gather small but specific labelled data sets for better performance
and clinical applicability.

anomalies in a gyroscopic
Sagnac interferometer which is normally used to calibrate the angular momentum
of a gyroscope. The spectral shift in the rotating gyroscope is explained with
respect to the longitudinal Doppler shift of the counter propagating beams in
the Sagnac interferometer.
  From the classical viewpoint, the gyroscope and the Sagnac interferometer are
two different devices with distinct physical phenomena. The gyroscope is based
on the angular momentum of a rotating body whereas the Sagnac interferometer
works on the speed anomaly (or anomaly of phase) in counter propagating beams
in a circular path. It seems unexpected that both devices show similar behavior
and similar parameters. In an earlier paper [L. C. Wang], we have shown that
the rotating gyroscope and the Sagnac interferometer are related through a
spectral shift function around the spectral anomaly of the Sagnac interferometer.
In the gyroscope, the spectral shift function seems to give the same information
as the angular momentum of the rotating body. In this paper, we report the same
phenomenon in the gyroscope with detailed analysis of the Sagnac interferometer
and explain the underlying physics with simple classical arguments.
  We believe that the unusual behavior of the gyroscope to give similar output
as the Sagnac interferometer may help the beginners in physics to understand
the basis of time and space around the speed of light. It may also give a
possibility to improve an existing gyroscope by proper adjustment of its spectral
anomalies for better rotation measurement.

  From a technical standpoint, iOCR's performance can be improved by training

an API-based service where the tabulation is performed remotely by a
reliable/secure service provider, with clear voting system architecture and
risk-limiting procedures in place.
  In addition to these technical issues, the use of iOCR will require election
officials to carefully consider the legal requirements governing the use of
automated systems in elections. Such systems should be tested thoroughly,
following a testing plan that is developed in cooperation with independent
third-party auditors. Testing should include both iOCR and any API-based
tabulation service.
  Finally, while iOCR and similar systems hold much promise for improving the
accuracy of paper-based elections, there is little research on systems that

leveraging optical mark recognition (OMR) systems in conjunction with iOCR to
significantly reduce the time needed for tabulating paper ballots.

formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as

a popular method for estimating the true
performance of machine learning models, allowing model selection and parameter
tuning. However, the very process of CV requires random partitioning of the
data and so our performance estimates are in fact stochastic, with variability
that can be substantial for natural language processing tasks. We demonstrate
that these unstable estimates cannot be relied upon for effective parameter
tuning. The resulting tuned parameters are highly sensitive to how our data is
partitioned, meaning that we often select sub-optimal parameter choices and
have serious reproducibility issues.

independent K-fold cross validations are used to assess performance. Our main
contributions are extending J-K-fold CV from performance estimation to
parameter tuning and investigating how to choose J and K. We argue that
variability is more important than bias for effective tuning and so advocate
lower choices of K than are typically seen in the NLP literature, instead use
the saved computation to increase J. To demonstrate the generality of our
recommendations we investigate a wide range of case-studies: sentiment
classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging and
document classification.

time by around an order of magnitude while still achieving competitive
performance once tuned. We also find that the best choice of J and K varies
across task and so advocate using a small set of J-fold cross validations to
select K, based on the average performance across validations, rather than
trying to pick K directly.

algorithm is orders of magnitude higher than the Monte Carlo approximation.

significance-testing frameworks and can make practical impact by selecting
better systems.

phase of binary evolution, in which two stars are enshrouded by the envelope
shed by one of them. Interactions between the stars and the envelope shrinks
the orbit. The CE can lead to mergers or to a subsequent phase of interactions.
Mergers may involve any combination of two compact objects and/or stars. Some
involving white dwarfs, may produce Type Ia supernovae, while merging neutron
stars may yield gamma-ray bursts, and merging compact objects of all kinds
produce gravitational radiation. Since CEs can arise from a variety of

involved, it is difficult to predict their end states. When many systems are
being considered, as in population synthesis calculations, conservation
principles are generally employed. Here we use angular momentum in a new way to
derive a simple expression for the final orbital separation. This method
provides advantages for the study of binaries and is particularly well-suited
to higher order multiples, now considered to be important in the genesis of
potential mergers. Here we focus on CEs in binaries, and the follow-up paper
extends our formalism to multiple star systems within which a CE occurs.

system, apply conservation of angular momentum during a common envelope, and
derive a simple expression for the new orbital separation in terms of the
initial parameters. This is valid for all $N$.

with previous results for binaries, but provides a new expression for the
merger rate of multiples.

the two companions crosses inside the Roche lobe of the envelope star, so that
tides may be active. We find that such configurations are stabilized against

the orbit of the two companions are outside the Roche lobe of the envelope
star, for which CEs may occur if the orbit is wide enough.

over-estimated the number of systems in which CEs can occur by a factor of
ten.

and the description of `what-if' scenarios that integrate complex sequences of

  Frisbee leverages a domain-specific language (DSL) allowing developers to
describe the target system under test (SuT) and the testbed layout in an
integrated manner. From this description, Frisbee generates a test plan,
activates the required virtual nodes (one for the SuT and the rest for the
testing infrastructure) and populates them with the corresponding software
components and configurations. After that, Frisbee executes the test plan,
providing a transparent and automated testing process for IoT applications.

implementation of an Intelligent Traffic System and an automation setup for a
Smart Home. The results show that Frisbee accelerates the testing process,
improves developer productivity, and demonstrates excellent performance in
detecting hidden errors and faults that other testing frameworks fail to

Existing methods typically insert actors into the scene according to a set of
hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in their ability to model the true
complexity and diversity of real traffic scenes, thus inducing a content gap
between synthesized traffic scenes versus real ones. As a result, existing
simulators lack the fidelity necessary to train and test self-driving vehicles.
To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model
of traffic scenes that eschews the need for rules and heuristics. In
particular, given the ego-vehicle state and a high definition map of
surrounding area, SceneGen inserts actors of various classes into the scene and
synthesizes their sizes, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two
large-scale datasets SceneGen's ability to faithfully model distributions of
real traffic scenes. Moreover, we show that SceneGen coupled with sensor
simulation can be used to train perception models that generalize to the real
world.

time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) is the ability to preserve
certain properties of the continuum solution, such as associated conservation
laws or other geometric structures of the solution. There is a long history of
the development and analysis of such structure-preserving discretisation
schemes, including both proofs that standard schemes have structure-preserving
properties and proposals for novel schemes that achieve both high-order
accuracy and exact preservation of certain properties of the continuum
differential equation. When coupled with implicit time-stepping methods, a
major downside to these schemes is that their structure-preserving properties
generally rely on exact solution of the (possibly nonlinear) systems of
equations defining each time-step in the discrete scheme. For small systems,
this is often possible (up to the accuracy of floating-point arithmetic), but
it becomes impractical for the large linear systems that arise when considering
typical discretisation of space-time PDEs. In this paper, we propose a
modification to the standard flexible generalised minimum residual (FGMRES)
iteration that enforces selected constraints on approximate numerical
solutions. We demonstrate its application to both systems of conservation laws
and dissipative systems.
  We show that it leads to residual-based global error bounds on the
time-stepping scheme, and that it preserves important properties of the
differential equation such as the conservation of integrals of the solution (in
the case of a system of conservation laws). These bounds are validated
numerically on a range of problems. In addition, we show that the
structure-preserving FGMRES (SPGMRES) iteration is equivalent to applying the
discretisation scheme directly in a certain way, under certain conditions on
the discretisation. This further illustrates the integrity of the discretisation
and helps to justify its use. In particular, it shows that it does not
introduce spurious degrees of freedom that would otherwise violate the
conservation laws of the underlying differential equation.
  Finally, we show that it leads to residual-based linearisation strategies
that are guaranteed to reduce the residual exactly in each time-step (up to
roundoff error), thus providing exact local error bounds on the time-stepping
scheme. These methods are safer than the standard Newton method because they
don't risk diverging when the nonlinear function is strongly concave. They are
also faster than standard iterative methods like Bisection and Brent because
they take full advantage of the structure of the discretisation.

the initial stages of the superbubble evolution, including the occurrence of
pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae. Our aim is to study the
occurrence of dust grain growth within orbiting dusty clumps, and in the
superbubble's swept-up supershell. We also aim to address the survival of dust
grains produced by sequential supernovae. The model accounts for the star
cluster gravitational potential and self-gravity of the parent cloud. It also
considers radiative cooling (including that induced by dust) and a
state-of-the-art population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. As shown
before, a superbubble embedded into a clumpy medium becomes highly distorted,
expanding mostly due to the hot gas streaming through low density channels. Our
results indicate that in the case of massive ($\sim10^7$M$_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds, hosting a super star cluster ($\sim5.6\times10^5$M$_{\odot}$), grain
growth increments the dust mass at a rate $\sim4.8\times10^{-5}$M$_{\odot}$
per core-collapse SN. In the case of pair-instability SNe, dust grains are
destroyed by the SN shock. The final-stage supershell, made of hot gas carrying
dust grains, can be observed as a pulsar or a compact star embedded highly
ionized gas nebula.
  Depending on the star cluster age and mass, the number of core-collapse SNs
ranging from 2 to 15 can occur while the stellar winds and supernovae powers a

generate pulsar emission at the characteristic frequency $\nu_{break} \geq
0.1$GHz is $\sim3\times10^{-5}$M$_{\odot}$. This limit is reached by a
supercluster with initial mass $\geq1.6\times10^6$M$_{\odot}$. In clusters with
lower masses, even those producing 15 core-collapse SNs, the generated dust

certain distance from an observer, e.g., $>$50m. Far3Det is particularly
important for autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating at highway speeds, which
require detections of far-field obstacles to ensure sufficient braking
distances. However, contemporary AV benchmarks such as nuScenes underemphasize
this problem because they evaluate performance only up to a certain distance
(50m). One reason is that obtaining far-field 3D annotations is difficult,
particularly for lidar sensors that produce very few point returns for far-away
objects. Indeed, we find that almost 50% of far-field objects (beyond 50m)
contain zero lidar points. Secondly, current metrics for 3D detection employ a
"one-size-fits-all" philosophy, using the same tolerance thresholds for near
and far objects, inconsistent with tolerances for both human vision and stereo
disparities. Both factors lead to an incomplete analysis of the Far3Det task.
For example, while conventional wisdom tells us that high-resolution RGB
sensors should be vital for 3D detection of far-away objects, lidar-based
methods still rank higher compared to RGB counterparts on the current benchmark
leaderboards. As a first step towards a Far3Det benchmark, we develop a method
to find well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset and demarcate the
far-field 3D detection boundary (50m). We then evaluate the performance of 3D
detection baselines on this Far3Det benchmark and show that even perfect
lidar-based baselines have significant room for improvement on far-away objects
that are almost invisible from lidar sensors. This is the first systematic
analysis of the Far3Det task and highlights the need for methods that can
effectively exploit RGB and learn rich appearance models to aid Far3Det.
Furthermore, developing AV software that uses 3D detections beyond 50m as
input will help establish a Far3Det benchmark through real-world performance.

in soft-tissue navigation. We focus
on laparoscopic liver surgery, where we register the organ model obtained from
a preoperative CT scan to the intraoperative partial organ surface,
reconstructed from the laparoscopic video. This is a challenging task due to
sparse and noisy intraoperative data, real-time requirements and many unknowns
- such as tissue properties and boundary conditions. Furthermore, establishing
correspondences between pre- and intraoperative data can be extremely difficult
since the liver usually lacks distinct surface features and the used imaging
modalities suffer from very different types of noise. In this work, we train a
convolutional neural network to perform both the search for surface
correspondences as well as the non-rigid registration in one step. The network
is trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly
generated, deforming organ-like structures. This enables the network to
immediately generalize to a new patient organ without the need to re-train. We
add various amounts of noise to the intraoperative surfaces during training,
making the network robust to noisy intraoperative data. During inference, the
network outputs the displacement field which matches the preoperative volume to
the partial intraoperative surface. In multiple experiments, we show that the
network translates well to real data while maintaining a high inference speed.
Our code and trained models are made available online.
  The network is shown to outperform the current state-of-the-art deep
methodology, DeepDeform, by registering on average $35.8^{\circ}$ fewer
rotation and $10.3~\text{mm}$ fewer translation errors during inference,
while also being much faster. Furthermore, we show that the network's
generalization capabilities are superior to a literature-minned FE model.
Finally, we demonstrate three different visualization techniques for
preoperative-tosubvolume mapping, (1) a direct visualization of the displacement
field, (2) a visualization of a mass-spring-damper system and (3) a
visualization using our previously published, optimal point distribution
network. The latter two provide a more intuitive but less accurate option.
Visualization 3 also showcases the benefits of using a robust network.

flow estimation. A second model learns a latent metric to distinguish between

intermediary feature vectors for the loss calculation. We use our proposed
benchmark to draw insights about the performance of the baselines and of
different models when trained using our setup. We find that our setup is able
to keep motion coherence and preserve local geometries, which many

One of the major obstacles that have historically delayed large scale adoption
of ANNs is the huge computational and power costs associated with training and
testing (deploying) them. In the mean-time, Neuromorphic Computing platforms

Neural Network (RNN), a spiking neural network with both theoretical and
practical appealing properties, as a general purpose classifier that can match
the classification power of ANNs on a number of tasks while enjoying all the
features of a spiking neural network. This is demonstrated on a number of
real-world classification datasets.

number of real-world classification datasets that rivals that of state-of-the-art
ANS and biologically inspired classification algorithms, while being much
simpler to train and configure than ANNs. The RNN's neurons and layers can be
easily visualized and interpreted, and can be tuned to fit a wide range of
computational power and accuracy requirements. The RNN's high accuracy and low
complexity makes it a great alternative to ANNs on a number of real-world
classification datasets.

biologically-plausible spike-based hebbian learning rule that reaches
state-of-the-art performance on a number of datasets both faster and at a
much lower energy than both ANNs and the basic weight update rule used
historically for the RNN. This learning rule further evidence the RNN's unique
neural architecture as the most suitable one for learning from spike trains.

also achieving near human performance on the GLUE dataset of natural language

for each one of its perfect matchings, there is another perfect matching of $G$
such that the union of the two perfect matchings yields a Hamiltonian cycle of
$G$. The study of graphs that have the PMH-property, initiated in the 1970s by
Las Vergnas and H\"{a}ggkvist, combines three well-studied properties of
graphs, namely matchings, Hamiltonicity and edge-colourings. In this work, we
study these concepts for cubic graphs in an attempt to characterise those cubic
graphs for which every perfect matching corresponds to one of the colours of a
proper 3-edge-colouring of the graph. We discuss that this is equivalent to
saying that such graphs are even-2-factorable (E2F), that is, all 2-factors of
the graph contain only even cycles. The case for bipartite cubic graphs is
trivial, since if $G$ is bipartite then it is E2F. Thus, we restrict our
attention to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A sufficient, but not necessary,
condition for a cubic graph to be E2F is that it has the PMH-property. The aim
of this work is to introduce an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic
graphs, whose 2-factors can be easily recognised, and whose study further
avoids the use of advanced tools typically required by the general bounds on
the number of odd cycles allowed in a 2-factor of a cubic graph.
  We characterise the 2-factors of a certain family of cubic polyhedra, which
include the 58-hedral dodecahedron, as consisting of two disjoint odd cycles

a novel technique for automatically
learning system call filtering policies for containerized microservices
applications. At run-time, Timeloops automatically learns which system calls a
program should be allowed to invoke while rejecting attempts to call spurious
system calls. Further, Timeloops addresses many of the shortcomings of
state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP, Python, and JavaScript. Timeloops has a simple and robust implementation
because it is mainly built out of commodity, and proven, technologies such as
seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers, with fewer than 500 lines of code.
We demonstrate the utility of Timeloops by learning system calls for individual
services and two microservices benchmark applications, which utilize popular
technologies like Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua modules), Apache
Thrift, Memcached, Redis, and MongoDB. Further, the amortized performance of
Timeloops is similar to that of an unhardened system while producing a smaller
system call filter than state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques.
Finally, we show that hardening the system calls learned by Timeloops with
seccomp-BPF filters provides resilient protection against
WannaCrypt-style\(^{1}\) attacks, even when an attacker has arbitrary code
execution inside a service's process.

the subsurface model from an initial
model by comparing observed and synthetic seismograms. Despite the potential of
FWI for high resolution seismic imaging, this technique is a nonlinear
optimization and may be trapped into local minima. Wavefield reconstruction
inversion (WRI) relaxes the condition that the wave equation associated with a
true physical source does need to be accurately satisfied during the iteration
process. Alternatively, extended source waveform inversion (ESI) introduces a
non-physical source deployed into the whole computing domain for matching the
observed data by synthetic data. The iterative process will move this extended
source to the physical source. WRI and ESI are formulated within the same
mathematical framework using Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method with a
special focus on time-domain formulation using extended sources, while putting
connections between classical FWI, WRI and ESI: both WRI and ESI can be viewed
as weighted versions of classic FWI. Due to symmetric positive definite
Hessian, the conjugate gradient is explored to efficiently solve the normal
equation in a matrix free manner, while both time and frequency domain wave
equation solvers are feasible. The most significant challenge comes from the
huge storage demand to store time-domain wavefields through iterations. We
describe two possible workaround strategies by extracting sparse frequencial
wavefields or by considering time-domain data instead of wavefields. Both
WRI and ESI are demonstrated on a 2D synthetic case and a real data case. For
the real data case, due to the limited storage, only time-domain data are
stored throughout the iteration while wavefields are computed on-the-fly.
Both WRI and ESI are able to provide a good seismic model in this case.
  Given the increasing computing capabilities, both time-domain wavefields and
records can be stored and the conventional time-domain FWI can provide a
superior result compared to WRI and ESI in the presence of real data.
Furthermore, a frequency-domain FWI for comparison is also provided.
  The main advantage of WRI and ESI is that they can provide updates even when
the mismatch between observed and synthetic data is due to instrumentation
limits rather than subsurface model inaccuracy. A practical strategy could be
to run a limited number of iteration with a relatively low quality data
matching in the initial iterations and then switch to a more conventional
FWI when a more accurate model is needed.

achieve optical nonreciprocity on a
chip by quantum squeezing one of two coupled resonator modes. By parametric
pumping a nonlinear resonator unidirectionally with a classical coherent field,
we squeeze the resonator mode in a selective direction due to the
phase-matching condition, and induce a chiral photon interaction between two
resonators. Based on this chiral interresonator coupling, we achieve an
all-optical diode and a three-port quasi-circulator. By applying a second
squeezed-vacuum field to the squeezed resonator mode, our nonreciprocal device
also works for single-photon pulses. We obtain an isolation ratio of >40 dB for
the diode and fidelity of $>98\%$ for the quasi-circulator, and insertion loss
of <1 dB for both. We also show that nonreciprocal transmission of strong light
can be switched on and off by a relative weak pump light. This achievement
implies a nonreciprocal optical transistor. Our protocol opens up a new route
to achieve integrable all-optical nonreciprocal devices permitting
chip-compatible optical isolation and nonreciporcal quantum information
processing.
  We also show that if a strong pump light is applied to the squeezed resonator
in our protocol, nonreciporal transmission of a probe light can be switched on
and off by a relative weak pumping light, corresponding to a optical transistor.
This indicates that our protocol can be used to implement a integrable optical
transistor.
  The proposed protocol has a potential to achieve integration of
nonreciporal devices and quantum processing functions on a chip. It would be
interesting to extend our protocol to show multi-channel nonreciporal
transmission by coupling the resonators to a photonic crystal array or
waveguide array.
  Finally, it would be interesting to extend our protocol to achieve
nonreciporal transmission of quantum entangled photons or polarized photons.
This could open up new possibilities of quantum computing and quantum
communication to be combined with a chip-based quantum memory.
  In conclusion, we have proposed an all-optical nonreciprocal device which
achieves a three-port quasi-circulator function from bidirectionally coupled
resonators and a mode squeezed resonator. With a reverse propagation of
single-photon pulse through the resonator pair, our nonreciprocal device also
works with a high fidelity.

study the joint effect of
immigration and a competition-dispersal tradeoff in the dynamics of two species
competing for space in regular lattices. Individuals of one species can invade
a nearest-neighbor site in the lattice, while individuals of the other species
are able to invade sites at any distance but are less competitive locally,
i.e., they establish with a probability $g \le 1$. The model also accounts for
immigration, modeled as an external noise that may spontaneously replace an
individual at a lattice site by another individual of the other species. This
combination of mechanisms gives rise to a rich variety of outcomes for species
competition, including exclusion of either species, mono-stable coexistence of
both species at different population proportions, and bi-stable coexistence
with proportions of populations that depend on the initial condition.
Remarkably, in the bi-stable phase, the system undergoes a discontinuous
transition as the intensity of immigration overcomes a threshold, leading to a
half loop dynamics associated to a cusp catastrophe, which causes the
irreversible loss of the species with the shortest dispersal range.
Quasi-transversal instability episodes occur in the approach to the disruption
threshold, leading to a mixture of deterministic chaotic dynamics and random
jump dynamics, which is exemplified by an abrupt increase in the variance of
k-intervals and a hysteresis pattern when immigration disappears. Our results
show that the exclusion of one species and the mono- and bi-stable coexistence
are promoted by the dispersal difference, while the chaotic dynamics and the
variance increase are favored by the difference in birth competition.
Consequently, the dynamics of this model is determined by the bidimensional
parameter space defined by the differences in dispersal and competition between
species.
  We argue that the framework proposed to study the competition between species
is general, and can be applied to any spatial pattern formation scenario. In
particular, the noisy voter model provides a specific case in which the
difference in dispersal can be turned off, thus allowing us to investigate the
role of the competition-dispersal tradeoff alone. Besides, the asymmetric
voter model can be seen as a precursor to the study of species involved in
mutualistic relationships. In such cases, mutualism can be simulated by
increasing the competition for the two species compared to a system without
mutualism, thus placing ourselves in a specific region of the dispersal-
competition
