movement of the Sun becomes main indicator of praying time, which can be
deduced using sundial. This kind of device probably permeated to Indonesia
during the Islamic acculturation. Since then, the development of astronomical
knowledge, technology, art and architectural in classical Indonesia are
partially reflected into sundial. These historical attractions of sundial
demand comprehensive documentation and investigation of Indonesian sundial
which are rarely found in the current literatures. The required spatial and
temporal information regarding Indonesian sundial can be collected by general
public through citizen science scheme. This concept may answer scientific
curiosity of a research and also educate the people, expose them with science.
In this article, general scheme of citizen science are discussed, its
application for sundial study in Indonesia is proposed as Suryakala-Nusantara
program.
  From astronomical point of view, understanding of ancient Indonesian
sundial, how it works, how it is made, and its development in time are needed
to understand its cultural significance. Modern replica of ancient Indonesian
sundial can be used as educational tool to introduce classical knowledge of
astronomy, physics, engineering, art, and architecture to the young generations
and public in general. These permanent exhibitions may persuade people to
recognize the importance of science, technology, engineering, art, and
mathematics (STEAM) in human civilization. Modern replica of ancient Indonesian
sundial can also be used as research tool to study solar physics effects on
ancient time keeper device.
  In conclusion, study of Indonesian sundial with citizen science approach
which involves general public, students, researchers, politicians, and leaders
can be strongly supported by permanent exhibition of modern replica of ancient
Indonesian sundial. This program can be initiated by several institutions and
funded by governments and NGOs. It is highly hoped that this program can
flourish and successfully answer several scientific and cultural inquiries
related to Indonesian sundial.

data and energy network and D2D
communication coexistence (DED2D) system. The DED2D system allows a base
station (BS) to transfer data to information-demanded users (IUs) and energy to
energy-demanded users (EUs), i.e., using a time-fraction-based information and
energy transfer (TFIET) scheme. Furthermore, the DED2D system enables D2D
communications to share spectrum with the BS. Therefore, the DED2D system
addresses the growth of energy and spectrum demands of the next generation
networks. However, the interference caused by the D2D communications and
propagation loss of wireless links can significantly degrade the data
throughput of IUs. To deal with the issues, we propose to deploy an intelligent
reflecting surface (IRS) in the DED2D system. Then, we formulate an
optimization problem that aims to optimize the information beamformer for the
IUs, energy beamformer for EUs, time fractions of the TFIET, transmit power of
D2D transmitters, and reflection coefficients of the IRS to maximize IUs' worse
throughput while satisfying the harvested energy requirement of EUs and D2D
rate threshold. The max-min throughput optimization problem is computationally
intractable, and we develop an alternating descent algorithm to resolve it with
low computational complexity. Simulation results show that our proposed
optimization problem can achieve significant throughput improvement as
compared to baseline schemes.

of heterogeneous cloud VMs, in this research, we also provide a model to
quantify the degree of suitability of each cloud VM type for various
transcoding tasks. The provided model can supply resource (VM) provisioning
methods with accurate performance and cost trade-offs to efficiently utilize

massless Dirac fermion Hamiltonian. In this work we present a semi-analytical
expression for the dynamical density-density linear-response function of
noninteracting massless Dirac fermions (the so-called "Lindhard" function) at
finite temperature. This result is crucial to describe finite-temperature
screening of interacting massless Dirac fermions within the Random Phase
Approximation. In particular, we use it to make quantitative predictions for
the specific heat and the compressibility of doped graphene sheets. We find
that, at low temperatures, the specific heat has the usual normal-Fermi-liquid
linear-in-temperature behavior, with a slope that is solely controlled by the
renormalized quasiparticle velocity.

obtained by plotting the compressibility (density of states at the Fermi level)
as a function of the electron density. This diagram presents a critical point
at finite temperature that separates a low-density region of long-lived
quasiparticles from a high-density region of bad fermions.
  In the bad-fermions region, the density of states vanishes at the Fermi
level, which implies a van Hove singularity in the charge-compatibility diagram
that originates from the spectral weight transferred to a gap in the density of
states by electron-electron interactions.
  Finally, we study the diagram for graphene sheets with a finite lattice
spiral disorder, for which the velocity along the Dirac points is reduced.
In this system, the quasiparticleic regime is suppressed by disorder for
electron densities larger than the average disorder strength. We argue that this
provides a theoretical explanation for an experimental observation of a
noninteracting system of doped graphene exhibiting long-range charge order.

freezing of the lattice agent that causes a van Hove singularity in the
density-of-states, which is equivalent to a structural transition that gives
rise to a system of noninteracting massless Dirac fermions with spin and charge
order, for average disorder strengths much smaller than the mean-square value.

retinal IKNM as a diffusive process across a nuclear concentration gradient
generated by the addition of new nuclei at the apical surface. The analysis
reveals the role of nuclear packing at the apical surface on the migration
dynamics of nuclei, provides a robust quantitative explanation for the
distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may have implications for
stochastic fate choice in this system.

nuclear imaging of a biological system can be used to provide insight into the
underlying physics that govern its development.
  This work may also have practical implications for the use of retinal
development models in the context of retinitis pigmentosa and other inherited
retinal degenerations.
  Finally, the methods developed here for tracking and analyzing the movement
of many tightly packed nuclei may be generally applicable to the study of
epithelial development.

opportunity to re-examine the relationship between nuclear position and fate
using powerful genetic tools in the context of a self-organizing system, and
to investigate the mechanisms that regulate the genetic and cellular
determinants of retinal development and homeostasis.

imaging strategies, analysis tools, and genetically modified lines, and set the
stage for further in-depth investigations of the cellular and molecular
mechanisms that govern early retinogenesis.
  We discuss the advantages and limitations of each imaging modality with
particular attention to optimizing imaging protocols and resistance
tethering to improve the success rate of experiments.

nuclear tracks that we have found to be broadly applicable to the investigation

standard epidemiological models, which require estimates for parameters such as
$R_0$. In this letter, we show that the effective value of $R_0$ in
super-spreader situations is significantly large, of the order of hundreds,
suggesting a delta-function-like behavior during the event. Use of a well-mixed
room model supports these findings. They elucidate infection kinetic modeling
in enclosed environments, which differ from the standard SIR model, and provide
expressions for $R_0$ in terms of physical and operational parameters. The
overall impact of super-spreader events can be significant, depending on the
state of the epidemic and how the infections generated by the event
subsequently spread in the community.
  We advocate a re-interpretation of the standard reproductive number in
epidemiology, distinguishing between the intrinsic reproductive number which
characterizes an infectious individual, and the effective reproductive number
which also takes into account the probability of continued transmission after
an individual changes environment. In a multiple-room scenario, the probability
of continued transmission, represented by the second R0, can be large (of the
order of unity) or small (much less than unity), depending on the state of the
evidemic and the design of the system. When it is large, infections can spread
independently of the intrinsic reproductive number, and a disease outbreak can
be facilitated (large impact of a single infected individual) or exacerbated
(clustering of post-exposure infections).
  Our results have implications for the management of infectious outbreaks in
multiple-enclosure scenarios, ranging from cruise ships to prisons, and areas
under lockdown. They can help optimize isolation measures, protocols for
removal of infected individuals, and reopening strategies in the context of a
contact tracing program.

the context of a super-spreader event. It may indicate small value for individual
infections, hiding the fact that a large number of infections are generated
through a single event. Thus, detailed information about the event is lost
when analyzed within the framework of a well-mixed population model.

Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic swept the
world.In China, COVID-19 has caused severe consequences. Moreover, online
rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic increased people's panic about public
health and social stability. At present, understanding and curbing the spread
of online rumors is an urgent task. Therefore, we analyzed the rumor spreading
mechanism and propose a method to quantify a rumors' influence by the speed of
new insiders. The search frequency of the rumor is used as an observation
variable of new insiders. The peak coefficient and the attenuation coefficient
are calculated for the search frequency, which conforms to the exponential
distribution. We designed several rumor features and used the above two
coefficients as predictable labels. A 5-fold cross-validation experiment using
the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function showed that the decision tree
was suitable for predicting the peak coefficient, and the linear regression
model was ideal for predicting the attenuation coefficient. Our feature
analysis showed that precursor features were the most important for the
outbreak coefficient, while location information and rumor entity information
were the most important for the attenuation coefficient. Meanwhile, features
that were conducive to the outbreak were usually harmful to the continued
spread of rumors. At the same time, anxiety was a crucial rumor causing factor.
Finally, we discuss how to use deep learning technology to reduce the forecast
loss by combining with external data, and how to design a robot to respond to
online rumors based on the forecast loss and a risk assessment algorithm.
Overall, our study demonstrated that the search frequency of rumors could be
used to quantify the flow of new insiders, and the peak coefficient and the
attenuation coefficient were suitable for rumors to be predicted. Most
importantly, our feature analysis showed that precursor features, location
information, anxiety, and rumor entity information were all important for
online rumors.

and the impact of the final adopted distance is to increase the estimated

help to break the sequence in the wide color spread of its member stars.

interest to subject this data to statistical analysis to gain more insights and

meet the performance requirements or lack simple and flexible programming
interfaces. To address this problem, we propose \emph{LifeStream}, a
high-performance stream processing engine for physiological data. LifeStream

query language support and performance by employing optimizations that exploit
the periodic nature of physiological data. We demonstrate that LifeStream

reflects its ability to solve real-world problems that require streaming
computations on large physiological datasets.

physiological data that achieves high performance and rich temporal query
language support. PhysioDS is a comprehensive dataset collection with
streaming workloads that helps evaluate and compare stream processing engines

neural network. Many loss functions have been designed to date, making a
correct choice nontrivial. However, elaborate justifications regarding the
choice of the loss function are not made in related work. This is, as we see
it, an indication of a dogmatic mindset in the deep learning community which
lacks empirical foundation. In this work, we consider deep neural networks in a
supervised classification setting and analyze the impact the choice of loss
function has onto the training result. While certain loss functions perform
suboptimally, our work empirically shows that under-represented losses such as
the KL Divergence can outperform the State-of-the-Art choices significantly,
highlighting the need to include the loss function as a tuned hyperparameter
rather than a fixed choice.

implementation of an efficient end-to-end framework for loss comparison is a
step in this direction. Our code is available at
https://github.com/AmanPriyanshu/LossCompare.

most commonly used losses in a unified format, making it straightforward to
compare and contrast different first and higher-order losses under a single
roof. ULF is available at
https://github.com/AmanPriyanshu/ULF.

evaluating the choice of loss function and we hope to present a more thorough
viewpoint regarding the choice of loss functions for deep networks.
  Finally, we highlight the necessity of re-evaluating the choice of loss
function in modern architectures including attention networks, transformers,
and pre-trained models in order to understand their full potential and
limitations.

strain-induced crystallization in unfilled polymers. This phenomenon
significantly influences mechanical and thermal properties of polymers and has
to be taken into consideration when planning manufacturing processes as well as
applications of the final product. In order to simultaneously capture both
kinds of effects, the model proposed starts by introducing a triple
decomposition of the deformation gradient and furthermore uses thermodynamic
framework for material modeling based on the Coleman--Noll procedure and
minimum principle of the dissipation potential, which requires suitable
assumptions for the Helmholtz free energy and the dissipation potential. The
chosen setup yields evolution equations which are able to simulate the
formation and the degradation of crystalline regions accompanied by the
temperature change during a cyclic tensile test. The boundary value problem
corresponding to the described process includes the balance of linear momentum
and balance of energy and serves as a basis for the numerical implementation
within an FEM code. The~paper closes with the numerical examples showing the
microstructure evolution and temperature distribution for different material
samples.

demonstrations are difficult for the teacher to provide. For example in
robotics, providing kinesthetic demonstrations on a robotic manipulator
requires the teacher to control multiple degrees of freedom at once. The
difficulty of requiring optimal state action demonstrations limits the space of
problems where the teacher can provide suboptimal or noisy demonstrations,
making it hard to learn a optimal policy. We propose instead to learn from
suboptimal feedback demonstrations, where the teacher provides optimal action
choices given the state they observe, instead of the state actions themselves.
We call this new problem of learning from feedback the "choice learning" problem
and show that treating the teacher's feedback as a reward function provides a
unifying perspective on existing algorithms for learning from reward feedback
and further allows us to develop new reward-based IL algorithms that utilize
the feedback. Our key contribution is that of rewriting the reward-based
ilibration framework of Reddy et al. to reflect the change in reward structure
and show that it allows us to learn optimal policies from reward feedback that
vary depending on the state. We perform experiments in both simulation and on
real hardware and show that our algorithms are able to learn optimal policies
from rewards that are suboptimal but helpful.

continuous phase
modulation (CPM) is quite robust to channel impairments such as phase and
Doppler shifts. Its implementation is on top of that simple. It consists in
multiplying the received baseband signal by its conjugate and delayed version
of one symbol period. However it suffers from a signal-to-noise ratio gap
compared to the optimum coherent detection. In this paper, we improve the error
rate performance of the conventional differential detection by using a delay
higher than one symbol period. We derive the trellis description as well as the
branch and cumulative metric that take into account a delay of $K$ symbol
periods. We then derive an optimization criterion of $K$ based on the minimum
Euclidean distance between two differential signals. We finally determine
optimized delays for some popular CPM formats whose values are confirmed by
error rate simulations.
  We also propose an improved differential detection scheme that takes into
account the channel impulse response. We then derive the corresponding
trellis description and optimization results.
  Finally, we show that for some specific CPM formats, the optimal delay for
the conventional differential detection is short (lower than 7 symbol periods
for the largest studied format). For these delays, the improved differential
detection (ideally or in presence of a channel impulse response) is almost
indistinguishable from the conventional differential detection.
  Keywords: Continuous phase modulation, differential detection, equalized
differential detection, delay optimization.

have brought new insights on the
final fate of massive stars, which are in contrast to commonly used parametric
prescriptions. In this work, we explore the implications of these results to
the formation of coalescing black-hole (BH) - neutron-star (NS) binaries, such
as the candidate event GW190426_152155 reported in GWTC-2. Furthermore, we
investigate the effects of natal kicks and the NS's radius on the synthesis of
such systems and potential electromagnetic counterparts linked to them.
Synthetic models based on detailed core-collapse simulations result in an
increased merger detection rate of BH-NS systems ($\sim 2.3$ yr$^{-1}$), 5 to
10 times larger than the predictions of "standard" parametric prescriptions.
This is primarily due to the formation of low-mass BH via direct collapse, and
hence no natal kicks, favored by the detailed simulations. The fraction of
observed systems that will produce an electromagnetic counterpart, with the
detailed supernova engine, ranges from $2$-$25$%, depending on uncertainties in
the NS equation of state. Notably, in most merging systems with electromagnetic
counterparts, the NS is the first-born compact object, as long as the NS's
radius is $\lesssim 12\,\mathrm{km}$. Furthermore, core-collapse models that
predict the largest kicks converge to the "standard" parametric prescriptions.
Kicks are crucial for the synthesis of NS-BH systems, and hence the merger
rate. The detailed simulation's kick distribution is too narrow, leading to an
underestimated rate. We recommend using kicks from 1D core-collapse simulations
in the context of galaxy distributions, or exploring alternative mechanisms for
NS formation that also deposit large kicks.
  Finally, using the models presented above, we predict that the population
inference of GW190426_152155-like systems will show a clear dependence on the
NS's radius and the natal kick assumption, with the former being the most
relevant parameter.
  We will derive new constraints on the NS's radius from the population of
confirmed BH-NS mergers, and discuss the implications for dense matter in
compact stars. Furthermore, we will investigate the effects of different
core-collapse models and supernova engines on the synthesis of merging systems
and will discuss the underlying physics linking core-collapse simulations to
binary compact mergers.

through 877k textual descriptions of inferential knowledge. Compared to
existing resources that center around taxonomic knowledge, ATOMIC focuses on
inferential knowledge organized as typed if-then relations with variables
(e.g., "if X pays Y a compliment, then Y will likely return the compliment").

agents vs. themes, voluntary vs. involuntary events, and actions vs. mental
states. By generatively training on the rich inferential knowledge described in
ATOMIC, we show that neural models can acquire simple commonsense capabilities
and reason about previously unseen events. Experimental results demonstrate

relation types lead to more accurate inference compared to models trained in
isolation, as measured by both automatic and human evaluation.

avoid "backtracking" errors, which are prevalent in existing methods that
explore the taxonomy. Our data and models are available online.

formulation of HHL suitable for the end-to-end execution of small-scale
portfolio-optimization problems on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL extends the hybrid
HHL variant with newly available quantum-hardware features: mid-circuit
measurement, qubit reset and reuse, and Quantum Conditional Logic (QCL). To the
best of our knowledge, NISQ-HHL is the first algorithm incorporating a
QCL-enhanced version of Phase Estimation executed on real hardware, the
trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1. In addition, NISQ-HHL includes a
novel method for choosing the optimal evolution time for Hamiltonian
simulation. Although this paper focuses on portfolio optimization, the
techniques it proposes to make HHL more scalable are generally applicable to
any problem that can be solved via HHL in the NISQ era.
  We show that NISQ-HHL can benefit from the exponential speedup predicted by
HHL, provided the matrix inverse is "classically truncated" at an optimal
point. In the best-case scenario -- where the optimal truncation point is
known -- NISQ-HHL can be $10^5$ times faster than the classical power method.
Additionally, we propose a "quantum-boundary" approach to indicate when the
exponential speedup starts to manifest during the execution of a small set of
full problems (as opposed to a large set of small problems). This approach
shows that, even when the speedup is not fully manifested, NISQ-HHL can still
provide a macroscopic quantum advantage in a few cases. Finally, we provide a
hybrid classical-hybrid quantum algorithm, which can benefit from a
superior-to-exponential speedup in a wide range of scenarios not solvable by
HHL. This algorithm further illustrates the benefits of the components of
NISQ-HHL.

T-dwarf to be discovered in 1995, and its spectrum has
been more thoroughly observed than most other brown dwarfs. Yet a full
spectroscopic analysis of its atmosphere has not been done with modern
techniques. This spectrum has several peculiar features, and recent dynamical
estimates of GJ 229B's mass and orbit have disagreed widely, both of which
warrant closer investigation. With a separation of tens of AU from its host
star, GJ 229B falls near the border of the planet and stellar population
formation regimes, so its atmosphere could provide clues to formation processes
for intermediate objects of this type. In an effort to resolve these questions,
we performed retrievals on published spectra of GJ 229B over a wide range of
wavelengths (0.5-5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$) using the open-source APOLLO code. Based on
these retrievals, we present a more precise mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$
and an effective temperature estimate of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K, which are more
consistent with evolutionary models for brown dwarfs and suggest an older age
for the system of $>$1.0 Gyr. We also present retrieved molecular abundances
for the atmosphere, including replicating the previously-observed high CO
abundance. While the retrieved absorption line shapes are generally consistent
with the expected effects of pressure broadening, the retrievals indicate a
much lower pressure than expected, likely due to an unresolved binary nature of
the host star. Further observational efforts are necessary to fully constrain
the system's properties, especially the spectral energy distribution, but with
these results along with previous dynamical estimates, we can begin to
assessment of GJ 229B's impact on the field of stellar and planetary formation.

an expansive wind outflow, often
constrained or channeled by magnetic fields that form a surrounding
magnetosphere. The very strong winds of massive stars are understood to be
driven by line-scattering of the star's radiative momentum, while in the Sun
and even lower-mass stars a much weaker mass loss arises from the thermal
expansion of a mechanically heated corona. In exoplanets around such low-mass
stars, the radiative heating and wind interaction can lead to thermal expansion
or mechanical ablation of their atmospheres. Stellar magnetospheres result from
the internal trapping of the wind outflow, while planetary magnetospheres are
typically shaped by the external impact from the star's wind. But in both cases
the stressing can drive magnetic reconnection that results in observable
signatures such as X-ray flares and radio outbursts. This review will aim to
give an overview of the underlying physics of these processes with emphasis on
their similarities and distinctions for stars vs. planets.
  We find that while there are many similarities in the processes that
generate mass and energy in stellar and planetary magnetospheres, there are
important differences in how these processes are initiated and in the
importance of background plasma properties. An interesting comparison is
between full-blown flares and more minor reconnection events such as cusp
flares at the Sun and possibly at Mars. While the driving stress and resulting
reconnection products may be similar, the much thinner Martian magnetosphere
means that the planetary case may more closely resemble the stellar case during
coronal mass ejections. Possibilities for such comparisons in other exoplanets
are being explored.

and, in turn, are regulated by Service Level Agreements (SLAs). In order to
ensure SLAs are being met, service levels need to be monitored. One technique
for this involves active measurement mechanisms which employ measurement probes
along the network to inject synthetic traffic and compute the network
performance. However, these mechanisms are expensive in terms of resources
consumption. Thus, these mechanisms usually can cover only a fraction of what
could be measured, which can lead to SLA violations being missed. Besides that,
the definition of this fraction is a practice done by human administrators,
which does not scale well and does not adapt to highly dynamic networking
patterns. In this article, we examine the potential benefits of using P2P
technology to improve the detection of SLA Violations. We first describe the
principles of a P2P-based steering of active measurement mechanisms. These
principles are characterized by a high degree of decentralized decision making
across a network using a self-organizing overlay. In a second step, we present
measurement session activation strategies based on these principles. These
strategies do not require human intervention, are adaptive to changes in
network conditions, and independent of the underlying active measurement
technology.
  We propose the use of active measurement mechanisms beyond their traditional
use for network QoS parameter assessment and define them as tools to generate
a stream of quantitative information regarding network performance. With this
viewpoint in mind, we present a framework for the construction of sliding window
performance profiles, which is crucial for the efficient monitoring of SLAs.
However, this framework requires the optimization of measurement coverage and
resources utilization. In this article, we present a set of algorithms that
build upon each other in order to achieve this optimization. These algorithms
make use of well-known active measurement technologies and a performance
profiling framework, which is also presented in this article. With this
integration, the construction of performance profiles across networks is
possible, leading to a more efficient SLA monitoring. Besides that, the
mechanisms that comprise the construction of performance profiles are
unrecognized opportunities for collaboration between networks, as they produce
beneficial information for network operators. Finally, our implementation and
evaluation showcase the practical application of the proposed framework and its
components.

neutrino oscillation experiments rely on detailed models of neutrino
interactions with nuclei. These models constitute an important source of
systematic uncertainty, partially because detectors to date have been blind to
final state neutrons. Three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers
comprise components of the near detectors of the next generation long-baseline
neutrino experiments. Due to the good timing resolution and fine granularity,
this technology is capable of measuring neutron kinetic energy in neutrino
interactions on an event-by-event basis and will provide valuable data for
refining neutrino interaction models and ways to reconstruct neutrino energy.
Two prototypes have been exposed to the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National
Laboratory (LANL) in both 2019 and 2020, with neutron energies between 0 and
800 MeV. In order to demonstrate the capability of neutron detection, the total
neutron-scintillator cross section is measured and compared to external
measurements. The measured total neutron cross section in scintillator between
98 and 688 MeV is 0.36 $\pm$ 0.05 barn.
  In addition, the neutron energy spectrum is measured in multiple ways and
reconstructed using a variety of analysis techniques. These include event
reconstruction, a method called NO$\nu$A-Neutron-tagging, and a method called
neutron-tagging. The agreement between the different analysis techniques and
with previous results is good.
  Neutron detection in proton-neutron final states will contribute to the
precision measurement of neutrino cross sections in solid targets. Based on the
data observed, we demonstrate the capability of 3D tracking detectors to
detect neutrons and quantify the improvement in measurement quality due to the
good timing resolution of the tracking detectors.
  Finally, using Monte Carlo methods, we estimate the improvement in neutrino
reconstruction resolution. For OSOS events, the improvement is around 10%, and
for OSCC events, the improvement is around 20%.
  In conclusion, with multiple analysis techniques and cross-checks, we have
demonstrated that 3D tracking detectors can measure neutron kinetic energy in
neutrino interactions with a high degree of accuracy.
  We also showed that such measurements will provide a means to refine
neutrino interaction models and reconstruction methods, increasing the overall
precision of long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments.

sticking forces between micrometer grains of chondritic composition. The data
showed a decrease in surface energy by a factor ~5 with increasing temperature.
Here, we focus on the effect of surface water on grains. Under ambient
conditions in the laboratory, multiple water layers are present. At the low
pressure of protoplanetary discs and for moderate temperatures, grains likely
only hold a monolayer. As dust drifts inwards, even lower sticking values are
expected. First, we measure the effect of multiple water layers on grains of
chondritic composition by increasing the relative humidity surrounding the grains
before measuring their sticking at room temperature. Second, we use the lab data
to infer sticking at lower humidity and estimate the effect of monolayer
surface water on the sticking at various disc radii.
  For multiple water layers, we find that grains become highly sticky,
surpassing the critical temperature for stickiness. This strongly indicates
that dust strands, so-called "chons," are formed during the drift in the inner
disc. When we infer sticking for a monolayer, grains remain sticky up to
synchrotron temperatures (~300 K). At even higher temperatures, the sticking
decreases to values suitable for strand formation upon collapse of the drift
stream, likely in the outer disc.
  Based on our laboratory measurements and interpretations, we conclude that
dust strands are formed by drifting chondritic grains both inside the snowline
and up to the ice condensation radius.
  Finally, we note that grains made from silicates only remain sticky up to
lower temperatures (~230 K), indicating that the presence of water is crucial
for maintaining stickiness at higher temperatures.

generation, imitation learning has been viewed as a vital direction in the
context of robot skill learning. In contrast to unconstrained imitation
learning which ignores possible internal and external constraints arising from
environments and robot kinematics/dynamics, recent works on constrained
imitation learning allow for transferring human skills to unstructured
scenarios, further enlarging the application domain of imitation learning.
While various constraints have been studied, e.g., joint limits, obstacle
avoidance and plane constraints, the problem of nonlinear hard constraints has
not been well-addressed. In this paper, we propose extended kernelized movement
primitives (EKMP) to cope with most of the key problems in imitation learning,
including nonlinear hard constraints. Specifically, EKMP is capable of learning
the probabilistic features of multiple demonstrations, adapting the learned
skills towards arbitrary desired points in terms of joint position and
velocity, avoiding obstacles at the level of robot links, as well as satisfying
arbitrary linear and nonlinear, equality and inequality hard constraints.
Besides, the connections between EKMP and state-of-the-art motion planning
approaches are discussed. Several evaluations including the planning of joint
trajectories for a 7-DoF robotic arm are provided to verify the effectiveness
of our framework.
  Which internal and external constraints can be learned by the proposed EKMP?
How does EKMP handle non-trivial demonstrations? How does the learned
trajectory change after enforcing different sets of constraints? These questions
are answered through the comprehensive evaluation studies.

the thermodynamic behavior of surface-grafted polymers in a wide range of
settings. However, the parabolic brush limit fails to describe polymers grafted
to convex, curved substrates, such as the surfaces of spherical nanoparticles
or the interfaces of strongly segregated block copolymers. It has been
previously shown that strongly-stretched, curved brushes require a boundary
layer devoid of free chain ends, requiring modifications of the theoretical
analysis. While this "end exclusion zone" has been successfully incorporated
into descriptions of brushes grafted onto the outer surfaces of cylinders and
spheres, the behavior of brushes on surfaces of arbitrary curvature has not yet
been studied. We present a formulation of the strong-stretching theory for
molten brushes on surfaces of arbitrary curvature and identify four distinct
regimes of interest for which brushes are predicted to possess end exclusion
zones, notably including regimes of positive mean curvature but negative
Gaussian curvature. Through numerical solutions of the strong-stretching brush
equations, we report predicted scaling of the size of the end exclusion zone,
the chain end distribution, the chain polarization, and the free energy of
stretching with mean and Gaussian surface curvatures. Through these results, we
present a comprehensive picture of how brush geometry influences the end
exclusions zones and the chain end distributions, and we report how these
features in turn affect the thermodynamic properties of strongly-stretched, curved brushes.
  We find that surface saddle points have peculiar geometry that favors the
end exclusion zone, and that the end exclusion zone is generally more pronounced
for brushes wrapped in a single layer about a curved surface (e.g. the outer
brushes on a cylinder or a sphere) than for brushes in a biconcave or parabolic
profile (e.g. the inner brushes on a cylinder or a sphere). Through a simple
model we also present how the single-layer geometry of curved brushes might
lead to mechanistically interesting chain configurations that are not possible for
straight or biconcave chains. Our results further indicate that surface
topology plays a crucial role in determining the chain end distribution,
polarization, end exclusion zone, and free energy of curved brushes. As such,
theoretical descriptions of curved brushes must take into account the complex
geometry of the host surface.

dictatorship mechanism in social
choice settings, we explore its usefulness in tackling various combinatorial
optimization problems. We do so by considering an abstract model, in which a
set of agents are asked to act in a particular ordering, called the action
sequence. Each agent acts in a way that gives her the maximum possible value,
given the actions of the agents who preceded her in the action sequence. Our
goal is to compute action sequences that yield approximately optimal total
value to the agents (a.k.a., social welfare). We assume query access to the
value $v_i(S)$ that the agent i gets when she acts after the agents in the
ordered set $S$.
  We establish tight bounds on the social welfare that can be achieved using
polynomially many queries. Even though these bounds show a marginally sublinear
approximation of optimal social welfare in general, excellent approximations
can be obtained when the valuations stem from an underlying combinatorial
domain. Indicatively, when the valuations are defined using bipartite
matchings, arborescences in directed graphs, and satisfiability of Boolean
expressions, simple query-efficient algorithms yield $2$-approximations. We
discuss issues related to truthfulness and show how some of our algorithms can
be implemented truthfully using VCG-like payments. Finally, we introduce and
study the price of serial dictatorship, a new measure of the cost of using a
social choice function that satisfies neutrality and is free of strategic
behavior.
  Keywords: combinatorial optimization, social choice theory, serial
dictatorship, social welfare, approximation algorithms, private function
evaluation.

evidence of being binaries from their PSFs, and an additional 22 targets were
worth further investigation. We were able to confirm 3 of the 12 targets as

Change Detection, only few approaches go beyond a standard benchmark evaluation
of existing models. In this paper, we propose a shift of focus from change
detection to change discovery, i.e., discovering novel word senses over time
from the full corpus vocabulary. By heavily fine-tuning a type-based and a
token-based approach on recently published German data, we demonstrate that
both models can successfully be applied to discover new words undergoing
meaning change. Furthermore, we provide an almost fully automated framework for
both evaluation and discovery.
  We achieve this by extending the previously used approach of visual
representation of the learned word embeddings with a threshold-based
methodology for evaluation and discovery. Besides a visual representation of
the learned embeddings, we introduce a frequency-based filtering of the
discovered words and a lexicographic validation of the results by an expert.
By doing so, we could reduce the number of noise pruned words by almost 50%,
resulting in a more realistic and useful set of discovered words.
  Our open source code and all discovered words for the BNC corpus are
available online.
  We also found that the previously assumed assumption that the token-based
approach is superior to the type-based one is incorrect and depends heavily on
the used data. By comparing the micro and macro F-score of both approaches
evaluated on the BNC and the NE corpus we show that the best performing model
depends on the used data and that no clear winner can be declared.
  Above that we investigate an ensemble approach outperforming both type and
token-based approaches by a large margin in terms of F-score.
  By systematically varying the size of the window and the number of clusters
we also show that the optimal parameter setting depends on the used data and
that there is no one-size-fits-all solution for detecting lexical semantic
change.

the embeddings of nearby time points are more similar than embeddings of

process is an open and challenging question in biology. Recent studies classify
the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by analysing the distribution of
a protein's planar projections using topological objects called knotoids. We
approach the analysis of proteins with the same topology by introducing a
topologically inspired statistical metric between their knotoid distributions.
We detect geometric differences between trefoil proteins by characterising
their entanglement and we recover a clustering by sequence similarity. By
looking directly at the geometry and topology of their native states, we are
able to probe different folding pathways for proteins forming open-ended
trefoil knots. Interestingly, our pipeline reveals that the folding pathway of
shallow knotted Carbonic Anhydrases involves the creation of a double-looped
structure, differently from what was previously observed for deeply knotted
trefoil proteins. We validate this with Molecular Dynamics simulations.
Moreover, we find that folding pathways leading to trefoil knots are
significantly longer than those of non-knotted proteins. We suggest that the
trefoil topology, and possibly other complex topologies, may be a barrier to
protein folding introducing additional energy minima along the folding
trajectory.
  We provide a public python implementation of our analysis and invite the
community to detect possible geometric features in the folding pathways of
known knotted proteins.

  The study of polymer flooding tapered cores is based on several idealized
models of mixing zones behavior, including the Koval model and the
Todd-Longstaff model. Depending on the viscosity function the limiting polymer
injection profile is rigorously derived. In the Koval case, the derived profile
is independent of the polymer concentration in the slug leader and depends on
both the polymer and slug concentrations in the tail. In the
Todd-Longstaff-like cases the polymer may or may not reach the last slug, and
the final distribution of the polymer depends strongly on the choice of the
viscosity function.
  For the case of finite number of slugs, several options of the polymer
tapering are compared numerically. Depending on the polymer flooding model, the
gain of the polymer compared to discrete slugs may be significant (several
percent) or negligible (less than one percent). In general, the gain from the
tapering increases with the oil recovery from a single slug and decreases with
the number of slugs.
  For the case of infinite number of slugs, the gain from the polymer tapering
is small compared to the accuracy of the numerical solution (of the linear
diffusion equation or of the nonlinear Koval model). Therefore, for the cases
when the leader and tail lengths are significant compared to the average
spacing between the slugs, the discrete slug model may be considered as an
approximation of the tapered core model.
  A rigorous analysis of the limiting polymer injection profile for the case of
transverse flow equilibrium assumption shows that the polymer is equally
distributed between the slugs in the steady state. Therefore, the concept of
tapering in this case is meaningless.

technology has to be carefully evaluated for a particular reservoir geometry
and fluid properties before any field application.

Hadronic emission from magnetically arrested disks (MADs) around central black
holes (BHs) is proposed as a possible scenario. Particles are accelerated in
the MAD by magnetic reconnection and stochastic turbulence acceleration. We
pick out the fifteen brightest radio galaxies in the GeV band from the Fermi
4LAC-DR2 catalog and apply the MAD model. We find that we can explain the data
in the GeV bands by the MAD model if the accretion rate is lower than 0.1% of
the Eddington rate. For a higher accretion rate, GeV gamma-rays are absorbed by
two-photon interaction due to copious low-energy photons. If we assume another
proposed prescription of the electron heating rate by magnetic reconnection,
the MAD model fails to reproduce the GeV data for the majority of our sample.
This indicates that the electron heating rate is crucial. We also apply the MAD
model to Sgr A* and find that GeV gamma-rays observed at the Galactic center do
not come from the MAD of Sgr A*. We estimate the cosmic ray intensity from Sgr
A*, but it is too low to explain the high-energy cosmic ray intensity on Earth.
We also estimate the cosmic ray intensity from our sample galaxies and find that
the predicted intensity is too low to explain the high-energy cosmic ray
intensity on Earth, unless Sgr A* and other low-luminosity nearby AGNs are
able to produce GeV gamma-rays in a different way. Finally, we estimate the
luminosity of cosmic rays from the nearest bright radio galaxy Fornax A. The
luminosity is as high as $1.4\times 10^{27}$ erg s$^{-1}$, or 0.07% of its
total luminosity. This implies that cosmic ray is important as a possible
mechanism for suppressing star formation inside radio galaxies.
  We also find that the GeV gamma-ray flux and the magnetic field strength are
correlated in the MAD model. This is because both the GeV gamma-ray flux and
magnetic field strength are proportional to the third power of the accretion
rate. Therefore, if we observe such a correlation in observation, we can
conclude that the GeV gamma-ray originates from the MAD.

wearable devices such as
smart phones and wristbands make it easy to get access to people's health
information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical challenges. Firstly, user data often
exists in the form of isolated islands, making it difficult to perform
aggregation without compromising privacy security. Secondly, the models trained
on the cloud fail on personalization. In this paper, we propose FedHealth, the
first federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare to tackle
these challenges. FedHealth performs data aggregation through federated
learning, and then builds personalized models by transfer learning. It is able
to achieve accurate and personalized healthcare without compromising privacy
and security. Experiments demonstrate that FedHealth produces higher accuracy
(5.3% improvement) for wearable activity recognition when compared to
traditional methods. FedHealth is general and extensible and has the potential
to be used in many healthcare applications.

  From a theoretical perspective, the behavior of quintessence as it enters
the apocalyptic region is surprising. Typically, a scalar field rolling
asymptotically linearly in time signals the beginning of the end of the
universe through decompactification, but the asymptotic behavior of our dark
energy field, which is dominated by alpha-cyclic contributions, is that of
cosmological constant. Nevertheless, the energy density still grows linearly
in time because of the dependence of the cyclic variables on the number of
particles created since the beginning of the universe. This suggests a
mechanism for the breakdown of the cosmological dynamics in which the
dependence on the number of particles is explicit.

dynamics for the many proposed inflationary scenarios that require many

would predict a primordial power spectrum with three distinct regimes: a

this invariant can be connected to electron transport along a nodal line, and

distribution to a more general class of distributions before providing them as
inputs to ML algorithm in the second stage. This allows the solver to
incorporate future direct bathymetry measurements into the flow velocity
prediction for improved accuracy, even if the bathymetry changes over time
compared to its original indirect estimation. We propose and benchmark three
different solvers, referred to as PCA-DNN (principal component analysis-deep

estimation process and/or extension of the range of applicable BCs, the
PCA-DNN solver has promising applications in predicting river flow velocities
from prescribed BCs, especially for systems with changes in underlying
geology.

challenging. In this work, we perform temperature measurements in a cylindrical

imaging (MRI) with the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency (PRF)

dimensions and agree with optical temperature probe measurements with an
average error of $\pm$ 1.5~$^{\circ}$C. We believe that the MR thermometry
methodology presented here opens new perspectives for the fundamental study of
mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds and in the future might be
extended to the study of reactive gas-solid systems.

gradient is achieved along the axial dimension, (2) the temperature gradient
along the axial dimension can be accurately mapped using MR thermometry, and (3)
the effects of gas flow rate and bed packing uniformity on the axial temperature
gradient can be investigated with high spatial resolution.
  We believe that this work has the potential to widen the understanding of
reactor design on a fundamental level and eventually contribute to the
upscaling of laboratory scale fixed bed reactors to larger reactor sizes while
maintaining or improving conversion yields.

study of reactive gas-solid systems and open up new avenues for the fundamental
fundamental investigation of heterogeneous catalysis.

work opens the door for further in situ investigation of gas-solid systems and
has the potential to widen our understanding of solid-liquid-gas
interactions.

characterizing temperature gradients in gas-solid fixed bed reactors is a
fundamental contribution to the field of chemical engineering. The open source

reinforcement learning to the evolving, open-world problems often found in
critical application spaces. Reinforcement learning solutions tend to
generalize poorly when exposed to new tasks outside of the data distribution
they are trained on, prompting an interest in continual learning algorithms. In
tandem with research on continual learning algorithms, there is a need for
challenge environments, carefully designed experiments, and metrics to assess
research progress. We address the latter need by introducing a framework for
continual reinforcement-learning development and assessment using Lifelong
Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a new, Unity-based, first-person 3D exploration
environment that can be continuously reconfigured to generate a range of tasks
and task variants structured into complex and evolving evaluation curricula. In
contrast to procedurally generated worlds with randomized components, we have
developed a systematic approach to defining curricula in response to controlled
changes with accompanying metrics to assess transfer, performance recovery, and
data efficiency. Taken together, the L2Explorer environment and evaluation
approach provides a framework for developing future evaluation methodologies in
open-world settings and rigorously evaluating approaches to lifelong learning.
  We present an integrated framework for developing and evaluating lifelong
learning algorithms, including a Unity-based first-person 3D exploration
environment called L2Explorer, a set of continuing task scenarios with
curricula, and metrics to assess transfer, performance recovery, and data
efficiency. The goal of developing this framework was to create a rich,
controlled, and challenging evaluation environment to support evaluation of
continual reinforcement learning algorithms and to promote development of
state-of-the-art evaluation methodologies in open-world settings. In contrast
to procedurally generated worlds with randomized components, we have deliberately
designed L2Explorer with modular task components that can be continuously
reconfigured to generate a range of tasks and task variants structured into
complex and evolving evaluation curricula. To demonstrate the utility of the
developed framework, we include an extensive set of experiments evaluating
different algorithmic approaches to continual learning, which helps to answer
fundamental questions about data efficiency, transfer, and performance recovery
across a range of continuous task scenarios. Experiment results illustrate the
importance of curricula in evaluation and show that some existing lifelong
learning algorithms have superior performance on continuing tasks relative to
baselines.

asymptotic state). These conditions can serve as early warning signs for a
sudden population shift in an ecosystem.

trajectory could be guided from a persistent MMO orbit to its asymptotic state

detected at least $100\,k$ time units before a large amplitude oscillation in
the full model. Thus, a large-scale ecological model with interference
competition exhibits situation-dependent delay before a sudden shift in
population dynamics. A set of generic global-attracting dynamics is observed
in a related system without competition, thus indicating that sudden shifts in
population dynamics can also be caused by the sole presence of interference

features a set of fences that interact with the coherence layer. Using the
model, we design an algorithm to analyze the reachability and check whether a
program satisfies a given safety property with the current set of fences. We
describe a method for insertion of optimal sets of fences that ensure
correctness of the program under such protocols. The method relies on a
counter-example guided fence insertion procedure. One feature of our method is
that it can handle a variety of fences (with different costs). This diversity
makes optimization more difficult since one has to optimize the total cost of
the inserted fences, rather than just their number. To demonstrate the strength
of our approach, we have implemented a prototype and run it on a wide range of
examples and benchmarks. We have also, using simulation, evaluated the
performance of the resulting fenced programs.

of the integers of size k with small sumset (of size close to 2k) then they are
very close to arithmetic progressions. Our aim in this paper is to strengthen
this by allowing only a bounded number of possible summands from one of the
sets. We show that if A and B are subsets of the integers of size k such that
for any four-element subset X of B the sumset A+X has size not much more than
2k then already this implies that A and B are very close to arithmetic
progressions.

additive groups of large prime fields rather than the integers. This allows us
to work with smaller sets still achieving similar results.
  Our proof combines pure combinatorial arguments with some higher-level
number-theoretic results, such as the hypergraph conjecture (in a weak form)

ultimately, the inverse conjecture for bilinear sums, in a weak form). We
attempt to motivate the different places where we need strong number-theoretic
results and discuss possible ways of weakening them in future work.

size of the sumset of A+X, possible generalisations to other settings and
different variants of the problem.

recognition in the dark.
In this work, we present our results on the ARID dataset. Most previous works
only evaluate performance on large, well illuminated datasets like Kinetics and
HMDB51. We demonstrate that our work is able to achieve a very low error rate
while being trained on a much smaller dataset of dark videos. We also explore a
variety of training and inference strategies including domain transfer
methodologies and also propose a simple but useful frame selection strategy.
Our empirical results demonstrate that we beat previously published baseline
models by 11%.
  We also demonstrate that our work is able to generalize to a variety of
real-world settings including a sports game and a martial art sequence.
Visualization of our results also demonstrate that our model is able to
supplement missing light by "filling in the gaps" with kinetic movements which
are present in the training dataset.
  Our code and trained models will be available at
https://github.com/hritam267/ARID_submission.
  This dataset and ground truth have been kindly provided by Joseph Ballan and
his colleagues from Google.
  We believe that this dataset, our workflow and techniques will be beneficial
to the community to tackle the problem of recognition in the dark.
  We hope this dataset and our workflow will help researchers to challenge the
existing baselines and also develop novel models which can generalize much
better to real world actions.
  We also hope that the dataset will help researchers to develop better
acknowledged metrics which can measure the performance more accurately and also
help to develop a standardized evaluation protocol.
  With that, we are providing a fully annotated dataset with ground truth
labeling and also baselines to train and compare.
  We are also open to collaborations and would love to discuss further and
possibly get feedback from the community.

the implementation of a Content
Addressable Parallel Processor using a FPGA. While Content addressable memories
have been implemented in FPGAs, to our knowledge this is the first
implementation in FPGA of Caxton C. Foster's vision of parallel processing,
particularly the notions of parallel write as well as the combining of output
values, which are usually missing in more typical CAM implementations, such as
the ones designed for network routing. The resulting CAPP is made accessible to
a host computer over a USB/UART interface, using a straightforward serial
protocol that is demonstrated using a Python-based driver.
  From an hardware perspective, the implementation is largely straightforward,
with the main hurdle being the parallel-to-serial and vice versa conversions
required for the interface to the host computer. The only really interesting
hardware detail is the parallel write logic, which is a fairly large and
complex state machine. While this logic could have been implemented as a
state-machine builder using a FPGA development board's "core store", I
preferred to fully understand how it worked, so I built it from scratch. The
resulting CAPP has a search time of around 50ns, is searchable while being
written, and has a cycle time of around 40ns when used as part of a pipeline.
It is fully documented, with a comprehensive user manual, and open-sourced
under a Creative Commons license.

Universal Texture Zero
(UTZ) model of flavour originally presented in arXiv:1710.01741, and update
them in light of both improved experimental constraints and numerical analysis
techniques. In particular, we have developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte
Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to exhaustively explore the UTZ's viable parameter
space, considering both leading- and next-to-leading contributions in the
model's effective operator product expansion. We also extract -- for the first
time -- reliable UTZ predictions for the (poorly constrained) leptonic
CP-violating phases, and ratio observables that characterize neutrino masses
probed by (e.g.) oscillation, $\beta$-decay, and cosmological processes. We
therefore dramatically improve on the proof-in-principle phenomenological
analysis originally presented in arXiv:1710.01741, and ultimately show that the
UTZ remains a minimal, viable, and appealing theory of flavour. Our results
also further demonstrate the potential of robustly examining multi-parameter
flavour models with MCMC routines.
  A key outcome of this work is a set of reliability checks on the UTZ's
parameter space that can be directly applied to other theories with similar
feature sets. We also extract a set of UTZ-like models from the same
fundamental origin assumptions, by simply altering the underlying representation
theory. These models offer minor modifications to the UTZ's parameter space,
and thus share a very high success rate in reproducing the correct number of
neutrino masses, as well as a realistic pattern of quark and lepton mixing.
Two of these models also predict a realistic value of the CP-violating phase
$\delta$ from the Standard Model CKM matrix, previously neglected in our
previous analysis. Finally, we show that the UTZ remains the simplest
representation of the GUT-scale $SU(5)$ D-quark lepton symmetry that also
predicts the correct number of neutrino masses. We have therefore enriched the
UTZ's already rich set of successes with additional predictions for ratio
observables and lepton mixing angles, and also shown that it remains the simplest
realization of a larger class of ``UTZ-like'' models.
  A companion numerical code implementing the MCMC algorithm used in this work
is available at \url{https://github.com/SHScotth/UTZ_MCMC}.

detecting anomalous data
samples in streams of data. This problem poses challenges that classical and
deep anomaly detection methods are not designed to cope with, such as
conceptual drift and continuous learning. State-of-the-art flow anomaly
detection methods rely on fixed memory using hash functions or nearest
neighbors that may not be able to constrain high-frequency values as in a
moving average or remove seamless outliers and cannot be trained in an
end-to-end deep learning architecture. We present a new incremental anomaly
detection method that performs continuous density estimation based on random
Fourier features and the mechanism of quantum measurements and density matrices
that can be viewed as an exponential moving average density. It can process
potentially endless data and its update complexity is constant $O(1)$. A
systematic evaluation against 12 state-of-the-art streaming anomaly detection
algorithms using 12 streaming datasets is presented.

anomaly detection methods or competitively in most cases and has the advantage
of constant update complexity at the same time.

any action is already known to the government. In this paper we attempt

  Building on original legal analysis and using precise computer science
formalisms, we propose demonstrability as a new central concept for describing
compelled acts. We additionally provide a language for whether a compelled
action meaningfully entails the respondent to perform in a manner that is 'as
good as' the government's desired goal. Then, we apply our definitions to
analyze the compellability of several cryptographic primitives including
decryption, multifactor authentication, commitment schemes, and hash functions.
In particular, our framework reaches a novel conclusion about compelled
decryption in the setting that the encryption scheme is deniable: the
government can compel but the respondent is free to use a random key.
  Can the government compel a respondent to perform a multi-factor
authentication? We demonstrate that this depends on the detail of the protocol
being used. If the protocol is designed such that the second factor is
computationally secret (i.e., it is supposed to be the case that the first
factor cannot be used alone to log in), then, we argue that the second factor
is not a foregone conclusion and the government cannot compel it. Otherwise,
it can.

others it provides only incremental ease of use (e.g., by caching a
authentication token after entering the first factor). We propose multi-factor
designs that eliminate the need for computational secrecy altogether.
Specifically, we introduce balance protocols that are inherently multi-factor
but do not require any computational secrecy (thus, a balance protocol can

  Baker's approach gives a PTAS on planar graphs, excluded-minor classes, and
beyond. For Max-CSPs, and even more generally, maximisation finite-valued CSPs
(where constraints are arbitrary non-negative functions), Romero, Wrochna, and
\v{Z}ivn\'y [SODA'21] showed that the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation gives a
simple PTAS for all fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes, which is the most
general "sparsity" condition for which a PTAS is known. We extend these results
to general-valued CSPs, which include "crisp" (or "strict") constraints that
have to be satisfied by every feasible assignment. The only condition on the
crisp constraints is that their domain contains an element which is at least as
feasible as all the others (but possibly less valuable).
  For minimisation general-valued CSPs with crisp constraints, we present a
PTAS for all Baker graph classes -- a definition by Dvo\v{r}\'ak [SODA'20]
which encompasses all classes where Baker's technique is known to work, except
possibly for fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. For fractionally
treewidth-fragile classes, we give a 2-approximation and show that, unless the
NP=ZK (which implies a breakthrough in cryptography), there are valued CSPs for
which no approximation with ratio better than 2 can be achieved in polynomial
time. For maximisation general-valued CSPs with crisp constraints, we extend
the SA-PTAS of [SODA'21] to all Baker graph classes, solving an open problem
posed by that author.
  All our results extend to "weak" global constraints, that is, constraints
whose scope may be restricted by other constraints.
  Finally, we define "local valuations" a new class of valuations which include
fractionally treewidth-fragile valuations, and show that, for crisp constraints
and local valuations, all maximisation finite-valued CSPs admit a LP-based PTAS
for which the number of subproblems of the iterative rounding scheme is bounded
by a constant.

scheme's accuracy solving a number of test problems, including the construction

inexact scheme is about three to four times faster than a high order
finite-volume scheme in the problems that we solve.

mean field game system with a constant diffusion term. We provide a constructor
for a high order Lagrange-Galerkin scheme that is capable of computing the

deep learning architectures are utilized for making critical decisions such as

applications, artificial neural networks (including DNNs) are considered as
black-box systems, which do not provide sufficient clue on their internal
processing actions. Although some recent efforts have been initiated to explain
the behaviors and decisions of deep networks, explainable artificial
intelligence (XAI) domain, which aims at reasoning about the behavior and
decisions of DNNs, is still in its infancy. The aim of this paper is to provide
a comprehensive overview on Understanding, Visualization, and Explanation of
the internal and overall behavior of DNNs.

Systems that evolve according to their Datasets and learning algorithms, thus
making learning processes highly data-driven. As such, DNNs offer challenging
opportunities for both applications of Systems Thinking techniques and research
purposes. Although there have been some efforts in applying Systems Thinking
techniques to analyze NNs, the literature in this field of research is not
considerable. In this paper, DNNs are regarded as huge dynamical systems and
Systems Thinking techniques are applied to understand and visualize their
complex behaviors. Different perspectives of interrelated components of DNNs

intermediate-mass stars, the rotation on the main sequence seems to be close to
rigid. As these stars evolve into giants, the core contracts and the envelope
expands, which should suggest a radial rotation profile with a fast core and a
slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, seems to show a surface
rotation rate that is faster than its bulk envelope rotation rate, in conflict
with this simple angular momentum conservation argument. We improve the
spectroscopic surface constraint, show that the pulsation frequencies are
consistent with the previously published core and envelope rotation rates, and
demonstrate that the star does not show strong chemical peculiarities. We
discuss the evidence against any tidally interacting stellar companion.

including the potential ingestion of a giant planet or unusual angular momentum
transport by tidal inertial waves triggered by a close substellar companion,

which takes a skill defined in a simulator and makes it applicable to a real
world environment. We call this process Cross Domain Skill Transfer (CDST). We
propose a novel learning algorithm for CDST, called Cross Domain Policy
Training (CDPT), which combines simultaneous learning of two different
environments with differential evolution to transfer a skill from a simulator to

approaches, and show that it achieves better performance on multiple tasks.

required by modern deep learning methods. It can be used to transfer any
skill-defined in a simulator to a real world environment.

the different regimes arising from this competition. However, they exploit
wavefunctions relying on crystal band symmetries, which tunneling interactions
are inherently sensitive to. Here we directly image lattice-aperiodic valley
interference between coupled atoms in silicon using scanning tunneling
microscopy. Our atomistic analysis unveils the role of envelope anisotropy,
valley interference and dopant placement on the Heisenberg spin exchange

by engineering in-plane dopant placement along specific crystallographic
directions. A vacuum-like behaviour is recovered, where the exchange is
maximised to the overlap between the donor orbitals, and pair-to-pair

dopant positioning. This robustness remains over a large range of distances,
from the strongly Coulomb interacting regime relevant for high-fidelity quantum
computation to strongly coupled donor arrays of interest for quantum simulation

because in-plane arrangements yield a nearly isotropic envelope, for the wave

innermost component of the CMS tracking system. The detector which was in

prototype readout system and a third disk was inserted into the old forward
pixel detector with eight prototype blades constructed using the new digital
read-out chips. Testing the performance of these pilot modules enabled us to
gain operational experience with the upgraded detector. In this paper, the
reconstruction and analysis of the data taken with the new modules are
presented including information on the calibration of the reconstruction
software. The hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual distributions are
also shown.
  Based on the analysis of the hit formation and reconstruction in the
prototype blades, the hit finding efficiency was found to be greater than
99.0% and the track-hit residuals better than 8 mm.
  The experience gained from the operation of the third forward pixel module
has been invaluable in the evaluation of the performance of the new CMS pixel
detector and in the development of procedures for the analysis of data from
the new detector.
  The full installation of the new detector includes 42 local detector
sections, divided into 16 central barrel sections and 26 endcap sections,
including 96 prototype blades. With the new detector in place, we can expect
improvements in tracking efficiency, momentum resolution, and vertex
reconstruction quality, which will have a significant impact on particle
physics analyses.

than that from the viewpoint of the horizon radius with the same condition.
These indicate that the shadow radius can be regarded a probe to reveal the
thermodynamic phase transition information of black holes. When the system is
undergoing the phase transition in two cases of the different non-linear YM
charge parameter values: $\gamma=1,~1.5$, the thermal profiles of the
coexistent big and small black hole phases with the temperature are presented.
Furthermore, the effects of non-linear YM charge parameter on the shadow radius
and the thermal profile are also investigated.
  We also investigate the geometric structure and thermodynamic phase
transitions of the charged AdS soliton in the framework of EPYM gravity. The
analysis on the thermodynamic phase transition shows that the introduction of
non-linear YM charge can improve the stability of AdS soliton at least from
the thermodynamic viewpoint. Furthermore, with the non-linear YM charge
introduction, the height of the potential barrier in the ergosphere increases,
which indicates that the existence of non-linear YM charge can not trigger the
star to fall into the event horizon once it enters into the ergosphere. These
results indicate that the non-linear YM charge can stabilize both the charged

find that it can change with different initial conditions of horizon radius.

effects of different non-linear YM charge values on black hole geometry. From
the viewpoint of shadow, the critical value of $\gamma$ is 1.5, while from

considerable volume of human-human dialogue data, especially when enforcing
features such as persona, style, or semantic consistency. In this work, we
challenge the conventional data-driven viewpoint and propose an operationally
defined framework that organizes system operations into states and transitions
based on a set of simple rules. We show that by carefully designing the state
transitions, an operationally defined system can maintain semantic consistency
and achieve a desired speaking style without using any of the common
fine-tuning techniques that rely heavily on large amounts of human-language

state-of-the-art baselines and a persona-aware model in terms of semantic
plausibility and speaking style, with a data requirement of zero.

The efficacies of pesticide
treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure on yield and profit. The objective of our study is to propose
a methodology to address the issue of an insufficient number of observations
using simulations and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield
through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of
strawberry disease management in Florida.
  For this study, we use the publicly available Florida strawberry dataset,
which contains information on yield, revenue, and disease pressure for various
treatment combinations. We use a simulation approach to generate a large number
of "trial" samples, which are then used to calculate the average treatment
effects and risks across all simulations. We then use the bootstrap method to
estimate the distribution of the average treatment effects and risks for each
treatment. To evaluate the efficacy of the treatments, we use the stochastic
efficiency with respect to a function methodology that incorporates disease
pressure using a quantile regression model. The results show that the rankings
of the treatments are consistent across different levels of disease pressure
for both average and lower tail outcomes. Without considering disease pressure
management, treatments would likely underestimate revenue losses due to disease
pressure. Our results show that considering disease pressure is vital in
strawberry management and that specific treatments may be preferred over
others based on disease pressure levels and location in Florida.
  Farmers, agricultural policymakers, and extension agents can use the results
of this study to evaluate the efficacy of different pesticide treatments for
strawberry disease management. The results can also help in developing
recommendations that consider disease pressure levels and location in Florida.
In addition, the methodology proposed in this study can be applied to any
field experiment with a similar issue of an insufficient number of observations.
However, practitioners should note that the results are based on a simulation
and therefore might not perfectly replicate the actual trial results.
Nonetheless, they can provide reliable estimates of treatment effects and
risks.

algorithms by computing the entanglement entropy after a quadratic quench and

finite size scaling of the XXZ spin chain in the thermodynamic limit by a
local calculation. This shows that our approximation is not limited to
macroscopic systems, but also valid in the thermodynamic limit.

the 2D ToricCode anyon model, we open the door for studying anyon condensates

weak equivalence principle (WEP) is based on
the minute measurement of the difference of accelerations experienced by two
test masses as they orbit the Earth. A detection of a violation of the WEP
would appear at a well-known frequency $f_{\rm EP}$ depending on the
satellite's orbital and spinning frequencies. Consequently, the experiment was
optimised to miminise systematic errors at $f_{\rm EP}$. Glitches are
short-lived events visible in the test masses' measured acceleration, most
likely originating in cracks of the satellite's coating. In this paper, we
characterise their shape and time distribution. Although intrinsically random,
their time of arrival distribution is modulated by the orbital and spinning
periods. They have an impact on the WEP test that must be quantified. However,
the data available prevents us from unequivocally tackling this task. We show
that glitches affect the test of the WEP, up to an a priori unknown level.
Discarding the perturbed data is thus the best way to reduce their effect.
Reasonable cutoff criteria exist for the two tests of the WEP that were
performed by the satellite during its four-year mission.
  We compute the maximum effect that glitches may have on the two tests' WEP
results, namely an error on the WEP test that may reach 2\times10^{-14} in the
strongest scenarios or be completely neglected in the least sensitive ones.
Although this level of systematics cannot be a priori excluded, it cannot
explain the small difference between the satellite's two test results that were
recently published [1,2].
  Finally, we estimate the effect of glitches on future tests of the WEP, and
in particular for the test planned by the PLASMA satellite [3], which will
operate in a similar configuration, but with a better signal-to-noise ratio.
Future studies will have to thoroughly investigate the number and characteristics
of glitches in simulated data corresponding to real observations.

(RE-TM) alloys with precisely
