9, Chile, and especially its capital
city, Santiago, suffered from widespread violence with public and private
infrastructure destruction. This work aims to expand an epidemiological
non-local model that successfully described the French riots of 2005 to
incorporate the topology of Santiago's subway network and explain the reported
distribution of rioting activity in the city. Although the model reproduced the
disorders' aggregated temporal evolution, it could not deliver results
resembling the observed spatial distribution of activity on Santiago. The main
reason for this failure can be attributed to the fact that the model lacks a
population displacement mechanism, which seems vital to explain Santiago's
unrest episodes.
  From a mathematical point of view, the proposed model constitutes a
non-compact infinite-dimensional system that converges to an equilibrium
solution as time increases in accordance with the degree of the system's
network topology. Moreover, it possesses a conserved quantity, which implies
the existence of quasi-equilibrium states that explain the system's slow
downward dynamics observed during the Chilean unrest. Finally, a least-squares
optimization method incorporating the topology of Santiago's subway network
retuned the model's parameters and successfully produced a pseudo-temporal
simulation that incorporated both the aggregated temporal evolution of the
unrest and a topological component explaining the system's behavior.

knowledge-amalgamation problem, termed
Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA). The goal of FedSA is to train a
student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and agnostic. Our motivation
for investigating such a problem setup stems from a recent dilemma of model
sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma and makes it one step further
since, again, the learned student may specialize in a new task different from
all of the teachers. To this end, we proposed a dedicated strategy for handling
FedSA. Specifically, our student-training process is driven by a novel
saliency-based approach that adaptively selects teachers as the participants
and integrates their representative capabilities into the student. To evaluate
the effectiveness of FedSA, we conduct experiments on both single-task and
multi-task settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedSA effectively
amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models and achieves competitive
performance to centralized baselines.

the rotation of solar-type stars goes
through different phases. Once they reach the zero-age main sequence, their
global rotation rate decreases during the main sequence until at least the
solar age, approximately following the empirical Skumanich's law and enabling
gyrochronology. Older solar-type stars might then reach a point of transition
where they stop braking, according to recent results of asteroseismology.
Additionally, recent 3D numerical simulations of solar-type stars show that
different regimes of differential rotation can be characterized with the Rossby
number. In particular, anti-solar differential rotation (fast poles, slow
equator) may exist for high Rossby number (slow rotators). If this regime
occurs during the main sequence and, in general, for slow rotators, we may
consider how magnetic generation through the dynamo process might be impacted.
In particular, we consider whether slowly rotating stars are indeed subject to
magnetic cycles.
  We find that kinematic $\alpha$ $\Omega$ dynamos allow for the presence of
magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotation regimes, but
only if the $\alpha$-effect is saddled on the tachocline. If it is distributed
in the convection zone, solar-type cases still possess a cycle and anti-solar
cases do not. Conversely, we have not found any possibility for sustaining a
magnetic cycle in kinematic $\omega$ dynamos.
  In the case of coupled dynamo models, anti-solar and solar cases share a
common forcing on the turbulent $\alpha$-effect, while magnetic cycles are only
possible in the solar case.
  Finally, in all cases considered, magnetic cycles are needed for the
generation of steady-state magnetic fields.
  In conclusion, if solar-type stars experience at least one magnetic cycle
during the main sequence, magnetic configurations leading to spectral types
like that of our Sun are preferred.
  If, on the contrary, magnetic cycles are unlikely for slow rotators, then
stellar models need to have a fast internal differential rotation (at least
10% from pole to equator) to reach a viable magnetic configuration.
  We also find that global magnetic polarity reversals are needed for a
magnetic cycle to be sustained in anti-solar cases.
  Last, note that in anti-solar cases, a monolithic magnetic structure
corresponding to the global magnetic energy maximum may change direction
between minima (if it exists)

evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the volatile sources and sinks.
Going from the deep interior to the top of the atmosphere, we describe volcanic
outgassing, surface atmosphere interactions, and atmosphere escape.
Furthermore, we address more complex aspects of the history of Venus, including
the role of Late Accretion impacts, how magnetic field generation is tied into
long-term evolution, and the implications of geochemical and geodynamical
feedback cycles for atmospheric evolution. We highlight plausible end-member
evolutionary pathways that Venus could have followed, from accretion to its
present-day state, based on modeling and observations. In a first scenario, the
planet was desiccated by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase. In a
second scenario, Venus could have harbored surface liquid water for long
periods of time, until its temperate climate was destabilized and it entered a
runaway greenhouse phase. In a third scenario, Venus's inefficient outgassing
could have kept water inside the planet, where hydrogen was trapped in the core
and the mantle was oxidized. We discuss the requirements for each scenario and
how they are tied into initial conditions and sources and sinks for volatiles.
These different possible histories highlight the complexity of Venus's evolution
and how its current atmosphere and magnetic field are the result of processes
occurring over billions of years. Understanding these processes is crucial for
constraining models of Venus's evolution with observations and may also provide
insights relevant to Earth.

processes for industrial chemical production. Here, we demonstrate the

average droplet size and charge. The use of ultrashort laser pulses enables
control of the amount of surface charge by the laser intensity. Moreover, we
demonstrate the surface chemical sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing
droplets of the isomers 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO in their ion emission and
fragmentation channels. Referencing the ion yields to gas-phase data, we find
an enhanced production of methyl cations from droplets of the 1,2-PDO isomer.

rise of GPU and TPU hardware accelerators, have allowed tensor network (TN)
algorithms to scale to even larger quantum simulation problems, and to be
employed more broadly for solving machine learning tasks. The
"quantum-inspired" nature of TNs permits them to be mapped to parametrized
quantum circuits (PQCs), a fact which has inspired recent proposals for
enhancing the performance of TN algorithms using near-term quantum devices, as
well as enabling joint quantum-classical training frameworks which benefit from
the distinct strengths of TN and PQC models. However, the success of any such
methods depends on efficient and accurate methods for approximating TN states
using realistic quantum circuits, something which remains an unresolved
question. In this work, we compare a range of novel and previously-developed
algorithmic protocols for decomposing matrix product states (MPS) of arbitrary
bond dimensions into low-depth quantum circuits consisting of stacked linear
layers of two-qubit unitaries. These protocols are formed from different
combinations of a preexisting analytical decomposition scheme with constrained
optimization of circuit unitaries, and all possess efficient classical
runtimes. Our experimental results reveal one particular protocol, involving
sequential growth and optimization of the quantum circuit, to outperform all
other methods, with even greater benefits seen in the setting of limited
computational resources. Given these promising results, we believe this protocol
to be suitable for enabling future enhancements of TN-based simulation and
machine learning methods using quantum hardware.
  From a theoretical perspective, our work provides a general-purpose TN to
PQC mapping, which is able to handle TN states of arbitrary quantum
entanglement~(including non-abelian and long-range) and can be tailored to
suit the specific hardware and computational settings of different PQC
implementations. We have made a purpose-built software framework available for
investigating the performance of TN-to-PQC mappings, which may be of use to
future researchers working in this space.

conservation properties. When properly implemented, conservation of total mass,
energy, and both linear and angular momentum is guaranteed exactly, up to
machine precision. This is particularly important for some applications in
computational astrophysics, such as binary dynamics, mergers, and accretion of
compact objects (neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs). However, in
astrophysical applications that require the inclusion of gravity, calculating
pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitively expensive. In the Fast
Multipole Method (FMM), they are, therefore, replaced with symmetric
interactions between distant clusters of particles (contained in the tree
nodes) Although such an algorithm is linear momentum-conserving, it introduces
spurious torques that violate conservation of angular momentum. We present a
modification of FMM that is free of spurious torques and conserves angular
momentum explicitly. The new method has practically no computational overhead
compared to the standard FMM.
  We test the new method with a set of rigorous tests, including isolated
rotating self-gravitating spheres, co-rotating binary clusters, and colliding
compact objects. In the last test, we duplicate the results from Duncan
Mergers (2019), who use particle-particle gravity, to ensure that our method
properly handles close encounters and mergers.
  We further verify that our method preserves angular momentum in realistic
simulations of planetesimals (macroscopic small particles) in turbulent gas
discs. Without any explicit damping, our implementation of Stokes' law (which
prevents physical particles from penetrating each other) maintains perfect
conservation of both linear and angular momentum in this realistic test.
  The new FMM is compatible with our implementation of gravity-based SPH, and
can be used in conjunction with any FMM algorithm used in other methods (e.g.
N-body). It represents a fundamental improvement that makes it feasible to
simulate certain astrophysical problems where angular momentum is a critical
conserved quantity.
  Finally, we note that conserving angular momentum in particle-based
simulations is such an obvious requirement that it is often left as an exercise
to the reader. We hope that our work will inspire a rigorous investigation of
the effects of angular momentum loss in both idealized tests and real
astrophysical applications.

transforming an audio
recording of a musical performance into symbolic format, remains a difficult
Music Information Retrieval task. In this work, which focuses on piano
transcription, we propose a semi-supervised approach using low-rank matrix
factorization techniques, in particular Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix
Factorization. In the semi-supervised setting, only a single recording of each
individual notes is required. We show on the MAPS dataset that the proposed
semi-supervised CNMF method performs better than state-of-the-art low-rank
factorization techniques and a little worse than supervised deep learning
state-of-the-art methods, while however suffering from generalization issues.
We argue that semi-supervised learning offers promising perspectives for
Music Transcription, as it makes the use of large datasets unnecessary.
  We make the following technical contributions : we adapt the convex version of
the CNMF algorithm to handle time-warped alignments ; we propose a second
algorithm based on the same factors representation, which uses the non-convex
optimization of a energy function inspired from Hidden Dynamic Model (HDM) and
make it run in linear time complexity ; we propose an initialization technique
based on beat tracking that significantly improves transcription accuracy;
finally, we leverage the representation learned from piano transcriptions to
detect harmonics in an acoustic transcription task and improve its accuracy.
  A separate study reveals that the audios used in Music Transcription datasets
often contain components that are not musical, such as noise and d.c. signals.
We propose a simple but efficient technique to remove them, and show on the
Jamendo dataset that it improves transcription accuracy.
  Finally, we demonstrate that the alignment learned in Music Transcription can
be used as input to a speech recognition system, to improve its word
recognition performance, and vice-versa.

configurations of rotating stars in general relativity. Having in mind the

of our own devising, in which we solve force balance equations to seek for the
positions of fluid elements assigned to the grid points, instead of the
ordinary Eulerian formulation. Unlike previous works in the literature, we do
not employ the first integral of the Euler equation, which is not obtained by
an analytic integration in general. We assign a mass, specific angular momentum
and entropy to each fluid element in contrast to the previous methods, in which
the spatial distribution of the angular velocity or angular momentum is
specified. Those distributions are determined after the positions of all fluid
elements (or grid points) are derived in our formulation. In particular, for
the models with the uniform entropy distribution in each component (usually
called polytropic models with Q=1), we can obtain the exact solutions by this
formulation. Furthermore, by assigning typical values of the entropy to each
fluid element in each component in general, we can also construct the models
with the uniform angular velocity distribution, which are preferred by the
stellar evolution and astrophysical studies. We also solve the linearized
Einstein equations to examine the validity of our formulation in the limit of
small deformations from the nonrotating configurations. In the numerical
aspects, we employ the second-order integrator for the force balance equations
and the fourth-order one for the Einstein equations. By overrelaxation methods
we can accelerate the convergences of the both sets of equations. We have
computed several models with the uniform entropy distribution (the usual
polytropes) and those with the uniform angular velocity distribution. The
results of our new formulation are in good agreement with the previous
nonrelativistic and relativistic studies.

high-quality labeled documents that are needed to train a model with acceptable
accuracy. We propose Selective Labeling to simplify the labeling task to
provide "yes/no" labels for candidate extractions predicted by a model trained
on partially labeled documents. We combine this with a custom active learning
strategy to find the predictions that the model is most uncertain about. We
show through experiments on document types drawn from 3 different domains that
selective labeling can reduce the cost of acquiring labeled data by $10\times$
with a negligible loss in accuracy.
  We also observe that the benefit of active learning in terms of accuracy is
minimal once the model has seen a reasonably large number of labeled documents.
To exploit this observation, we propose Cost-Effective Active Learning (CEAL)
algorithms that use the uncertainty alone to select instances for labeling.
CEAL algorithms are simple to implement, and they provide a nice switch point
between manual labeling and automatic extraction tools. Experiments confirm that
CEAL algorithms can reduce the labeling cost by $5\times$ with a noticeable gain
in accuracy.
  Finally, we propose Pool-Based Active Learning (PBAL), a novel labeling
protocol that reduces the cost of active learning by using a pool of documents
instead of a pool of instances. PBAL is easy to implement, and it provides a
nice switch point between manual labeling and automatic extraction tools. Experiments
show that PBAL can reduce the labeling cost by $2\times$ with a noticeable gain
in accuracy.
  In summary, our work shows that selective labeling, cost-effective active
learning, and pool-based active learning are novel techniques that can significantly
reduce the cost of acquiring labeled documents allowing to build higher
accuracy automatic extraction models.

over the territory is a fundamental step to
provide 5G connectivity. However, little efforts have been done so far on the
exposure assessment from 5G cellular towers over young people and "sensitive"
buildings, like schools and medical centers. To face such issues, we provide a
sound methodology for the numerical evaluation of 5G (and pre-5G) downlink
exposure over children, teenagers, schools and medical centers. We then apply
the proposed methodology over two real scenarios. Results reveal that the
exposure from 5G cellular towers will increase in the forthcoming years, in
parallel with the growth of the 5G adoption levels. However, the exposure
levels are well below the maximum ones defined by international regulations.
Moreover, the exposure over children and teenagers is similar to the one of the
whole population, while the exposure over schools and medical centers can be
lower than the one of the whole set of buildings. Finally, the exposure from 5G
is strongly lower than the pre-5G one when the building attenuation is
introduced and a maturity adoption level for 5G is assumed.
  From the regulatory point of view, the evaluation of the exposure from 5G
cellular towers requires the definition of specific reference levels for 5G
(\ie not a continuation of the 4G ones). Furthermore, exposure assessments
should not be limited to 5G, but should consider the overall wireless
infrastructure (including pre-5G cells) and all the relevant building types.
This is in line with the aim of protecting the health of young people and
other vulnerable populations, for which specific protection levels should be
defined. Finally, the adoption levels for 5G and pre-5G assume a geographical
variation and should be considered as random variables. Therefore, we recommend
to present statistics on the exposure for each adoption level assumption, in
order to make the numerical results more robust.
  As a concluding remark, the proposed methodology can be applied to any type
of cellular technology and building types, and it is not limited to downlink
exposure assessment. Moreover, the proposed methodology can be extended to
evaluate the exposure from a large number of cellular towers, instead of the
low number of examples here considered.

a complex task
for autonomous mobile platforms. Especially when conditions worsen, typical
sensor modalities may fail to operate optimally and subsequently provide inapt
input for safe navigation control. In this study, we present an approach for
the navigation of a dynamic indoor environment with a mobile platform with a
single or several sonar sensors using a layered control system. These sensors
can operate in conditions such as rain, fog, dust, or dirt. The different
control layers, such as collision avoidance and corridor following behavior,
are activated based on acoustic flow queues in the fusion of the sonar images.
The novelty of this work is allowing these sensors to be freely positioned on
the mobile platform and providing the framework for designing the optimal
navigational outcome based on a zoning system around the mobile platform.
Presented in this paper is the acoustic flow model used, as well as the design
of the layered controller. Next to validation in simulation, an implementation
is presented and validated in a real office environment using a real mobile
platform with one, two, or three sonar sensors in real time with 2D navigation.
Multiple sensor layouts were validated in both the simulation and real
experiments to demonstrate that the modular approach for the controller and
sensor fusion works optimally. The results show that with this model and
technology it is possible to achieve stable and safe navigation in a dynamic
indoor environment.

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA) as a typical robust
alternative of the conventional PCA has enjoyed great popularity over the past
years. In this work, we consider a rotationally invariant L1-PCA, which is
hardly studied in the literature. To tackle it, we propose a proximal
alternating linearized minimization method with a nonlinear extrapolation for
solving its two-block reformulation. Moreover, we show that the proposed method
converges at least linearly to a limiting critical point of the reformulated
problem. Such a point is proved to be a critical point of the original problem
under a condition imposed on the step size. Finally, we conduct numerical
experiments on both synthetic and real datasets to support our theoretical
developments and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.
  As L1-PCA is an eigenvector problem, directly applying a first-order
methodology to compute the principal vectors that implement the maximum
possible separation between the projected data can be quite challenging. To
relax this hard constraint on the eigenvectors, we further propose two
optimization problems, whose solutions are approximate eigenvectors and
linearly convergent to the desired principal vectors under certain conditions
on the data distribution. These problems can be efficiently solved via our
proposed L1-PCA algorithm. Numerical experiments show that the principal
vectors computed by our approach are better than those obtained by the Riemann
Trust-Region Method and the existing L1-PCA algorithms.

Variables (CV), known as asynchronous
polars, are still relatively poorly understood. An asynchronous polar is a
polar in which the spin period of the white dwarf is either shorter or longer
than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have
intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. We compared standard and asynchronous
polars in order to examine the relationship between a CV's synchronization
status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,
we find that the asynchronous polars may, indeed, have harder spectra, but that
the result is not statistically significant.
  A correction factor is applied to the standard polars to account for the
selection effects of the large-area surveys in which they were discovered. The
result is consistent with the asynchronous polars being a subclass of the
standards, rather than a separate class with harder spectra.
  Furthermore, the asynchronous polars have a range of spectral shapes, including
one soft spectrum and one that is significantly harder than the rest, making it
difficult to draw conclusions about the subclass as a whole.
  Finally, the asynchronous polars appear to have higher accretion rates than the
standards, which may be responsible for their apparently harder spectra.
  Further observation is needed to fully understand this fascinating subclass
of CVs.

mobile robots. The map is the core component to achieve this. Most map
representations rely on drift-free state estimation and provide a global metric
map to navigate. However, in large-scale real-world applications, it's hard to
prohibit drifts and compose a globally consistent map quickly. In this paper, a
novel representation named, HiTMap, is proposed to enhance the existing map
representations. The central idea is to adopt a submap-based hierarchical
topology rather than a global metric map so that only a local metric map is
maintained for obstacle avoidance which ensures the lightweight of the
representation. To guide the robots navigate into unknown spaces, frontiers are
detected and attached to the map as an attribute. We also develop a path
planning module to evaluate the feasibility and efficiency of our map
representation. The system is validated in a simulation environment and a
demonstration in the real world is conducted. In addition, the HiTMap is made
available open-source.
  From the results, our proposed map representation outperforms the Latin Cross
pattern in terms of the number of submaps and the detecting capability of
frontiers. Besides, the HiTMap can improve the path planning's convergence and
efficiency. Furthermore, the HiTMap can adapt to different scanning patterns and
reduce the needed memory.
  In summary, the HiTMap offers a novel map representation that enables robots
to efficiently navigate in unknown environments by balancing localization and
path planning. By attaching detected frontiers as attributes and maintaining a
Hierarchical Topology, the map can reduce drifts and improve the overall
performance.
  Future work includes the optimization of the submap merging strategy and the
adaptation of the HiTMap to graph-based methods for localization and mapping. In
addition, we plan to evaluate the HiTMap in real-world large-scale scenarios,

too inefficient for
SIMD high-performance computing, despite the fact that many important HPC
applications have an inherent object structure. On SIMD accelerators, including
GPUs, this is mainly due to performance problems with memory allocation and
memory access: There are a few libraries that support parallel memory
allocation directly on accelerator devices, but all of them suffer from
uncoalesed memory accesses.
  We discovered a broad class of object-oriented programs with many important
real-world applications that can be implemented efficiently on massively
parallel SIMD accelerators. We call this class Single-Method Multiple-Objects
(SMMO), because parallelism is expressed by running a method on all objects of
a type.
  To make fast GPU programming available to average programmers, we developed
DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework for SMMO applications. DynaSOAr consists of (1) a
fully-parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator, (2) a data layout DSL and
(3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. DynaSOAr achieves performance
superior to state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by controlling both memory
allocation and memory access.
  DynaSOAr improves the usage of allocated memory with a Structure of Arrays
data layout and achieves low memory fragmentation through efficient management
of free and allocated memory blocks with lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps.
Contrary to other allocators, it achieves this while keeping memory accesses
coalesced. DynaSOAr is 1.5x to 4.5x faster than the state-of-the-art memory
allocators c10t3, pmr-blasted, blowfish, and parallel-bitmap-memory-allocation
pbma and supports parallel deallocation with high performance.
  We demonstrate that DynaSOAr is not a specialized solver for a particular
problem, but instead, it is generic enough to be used as a building block in
multiple GPU algorithms, including parallel sorting, parallel prefix sum,
parallel reduce, and physical simulation (cloth and water).
  In conclusion, DynaSOAr is the first parallel memory allocator that can
utilize the full computational power of modern GPUs.
  We hope that DynaSOAr will lead to a re-evaluation of object-oriented
programming on SIMD accelerators and possibly lead to algorithms that are
specific to SIMD accelerators but cannot be expressed any other way.

equilibrium of the ICM is believed to be partially ensured by non-thermal
pressure support, notably the dissipation of energy through turbulent motions.
Accurate mapping of turbulence using X-ray emission lines is challenging due to
the lack of spatially-resolved spectroscopy. Only future instruments such as
the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on Athena will have the spatial and
spectral resolution to quantitatively investigate the ICM turbulence at all
scales. Powerful diagnostics for these studies are line shift and the line
broadening maps, and the second-order structure function. When estimating these
quantities, instruments will be limited by uncertainties of their measurements,
and by the sample variance (aka cosmic variance) of the observation. We extend
here the formalism started in our companion paper I to include the effect of
statistical uncertainties in the estimation of these line diagnostics, in
particular for structure functions. We demonstrate that statistics contribute
to the total variance through different terms, which depend on the geometry of
the detector, the spatial binning and the nature of the turbulent field. These
terms are important when probing the small scales of the turbulence. An
application of these equations is performed for the X-IFU, using synthetic
turbulent velocity maps of a Coma-like cluster. We show that statistics
dominate the total variance on the small scales (less than 10 kpc), while the
sample variance is more important on the large scales (from a few tens to a few
hundreds kpc). This justifies the use of realistic statistical models in the
formation of mock maps used for simulation studies.

can be easily translated to any spatially-resolved observation of a cluster of
galaxies. They are, therefore, applicable to mock map simulations based on
cluster physics models, to better quantify the effects of statistics on the
line diagnostics and to improve the realism of these simulations.
  Finally, we recommend that future studies on the ICM turbulence include
realistic statistical models of the data to accurately quantify the effects of
statistics on the line diagnostics, and that these studies should be extended to
examine how statistics affect the estimation of turbulence-related quantities
from mock map simulations.

theory was initiated by
Erd\H{o}s and Galvin in 1993. In this paper we are concerned with the following
problem: given a fixed finite graph $F$, what is the largest value of $\lambda$
such that every 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ contains
a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor whose vertex set has upper density at least
$\lambda$?
  Here we prove a new lower bound for this problem. For some choices of $F$,
including cliques and odd cycles, this new bound is sharp, as it matches an
older upper bound. For the particular case where $F$ is a triangle, we also
give an explicit lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}=0.62203\dots$, improving
the previous best bound of 3/5.
  Our approach combines infinitary Ramsey theory with problems in finite
geometry. The main idea is to exploit the large size (in terms of Ramsey
theory) of some finite graphs associated with the general position of lines in
$\mathbb{R}^2$. Let us say that a graph $G$ has \emph{much complexity} if it
contains a large simplifiable edge-set $E(G)$ such that every 2-edge-coloring
of $E(G)$ contains a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor. Our general position
linearity technique shows that many graphs have much complexity. We convey this
idea from the finite setting of general position lines to the infinite world of
Ramsey theory.
  Another important contribution of this paper is to show how to turn
non-ramseyic results into ramseyic ones. For example, the infinite set $I$ with
upper density $\lambda$ may contain an infinite $F$-factor whenever we can find
a finite $F$-factor whose vertices have upper density at least $\lambda-1$.
This allows us to transfer lower bounds from finite to infinite settings.
Finally, we give two explicit constructions of infinite $F$-factors containing
monochromatic infinite $F'$-factors for appropriate choices of $F$ and $F'$.
While these constructions are trivial in a finite setting, they require some
care in the infinite case.
  In the final section we also register some natural open problems for future
research.

is a ring-like structure sitting at the
center of the Milky Way. Using the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from the APEX
Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy (ATLASGAL), we study the anisotropy
of the density structure of the gas in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using
the 2D correlation function. To quantify the spatial anisotropy, we define the
critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$, as well as the anisotropy parameter
$A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$. We find that the density structure
is strongly anisotropic at the large scale (~ 100 pc), and the degree of
spatial anisotropy decreases with the decreasing scale. At the scale of ~ 10
pc, the structure is still mildly anisotropic. In our analyses, we provide a
quantitative description of the anisotropic density structure of gas in the
CMZ, and the formalism can be applied to different regions to study their
differences.
  We find that the strong large-scale anisotropy is mainly caused by the
Galactic bar, which pushes gas to flow along the bar and leads to the
upstream overdensity and downstream underdensity. The main effect of the
anisotropy at the scale of ~ 10 pc is not clear, but it may be caused by the
dense star cluster and massive star formation region embedded in gas.
Therefore, the typical scale of the anisotropy caused by massive star
formation is similar to that of supernova feedback (~ 10 pc). In addition,
the underdevelopment of star formation at the low-mass end may also be due to
the underdevelopment of density structure at the low-density end.
  Finally, we discuss how the anisotropy affects star formation. In regions
with strong anisotropy, the star formation is underdevelopment at the
low-mass end. Therefore, the anisotropy may be a physical factor that affects
star formation.
  Based on the above discussions, we conclude that the anisotropy of density
structure is crucial for understanding the evolution of gas in the CMZ.
Furthermore, the anisotropy may be a crucial factor that affects star formation
in the CMZ.

out of time correlator as a function of noise coming from an amplitude damping
error channel and a generalized Pauli channel decoherence channel for both
qubits and qutrits. For the same error in determination of the mass, the qutrit
simulations can tolerate 10 to 100x larger gate noise than a qubit simulation.
We find that 2-site qutrit simulations can determine a mass gap within an
error of $\pm 0.1 s^{-1}$ in noise up to $10^{-5}$. This suggests that for
quantum simulations of strongly coupled field theories, the advantage of
using qudits over qubits is not simply a result of the large multiplexing
advantage, but is instead a fundamental result of the structure of quantum
fields.

errors, the simulation can be made more robust by increasing the total Hamiltonian
evolution time before measuring. This is in contrast to classical simulations
where increasing the computation time generally just increases the noise in the
result.
  Finally, by varying the Hamiltonian evolution time and noise level, we are
able to empirically determine a set of parameters for a mock trial of a
quantum-to-classical continuation procedure for the mass gap.

been an unsolved question of high-energy astrophysics. One approach for solving
this puzzle is to correlate UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, since neutrinos
are a direct probe of hadronic interactions of cosmic rays and are not
deflected by magnetic fields. In this paper, we present three different
approaches for correlating the arrival directions of neutrinos with the arrival
directions of UHECRs. The neutrino data is provided by the IceCube Neutrino
Observatory and ANTARES, while the UHECR data with energies above $\sim$50 EeV
is provided by the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. All
experiments provide increased statistics and improved reconstructions with
respect to our previous results reported in 2015. The first analysis uses a
high-statistics neutrino sample optimized for point-source searches to search
for excesses of neutrinos clustering in the vicinity of UHECR directions. The
second analysis searches for an excess of UHECRs in the direction of the
highest-energy neutrinos. The third analysis searches for an excess of pairs of
UHECRs and highest-energy neutrinos on different angular scales. None of the
analyses has found a significant excess, and previously reported
over-fluctuations are reduced in significance. Based on these results, we
update our previous flux model-based approach with a new method taking into
account the dependence of the flux of UHECR energies and directions.
  Using the new lower-flux upper limits, the probability of an accidental
overlap of a neutrino with a UHECR within 0.3$^\circ$ is $>$10\% for all
energies, while the probability of an accidental overlap within 1$^\circ$ is
$<$50% for all energies. Additionally, we find an excess of pairs within
0.3$^\circ$ at moderate energies (E$\sim$40 EeV) with a significance of 3.2
$\sigma$. While the result does not reach the required 5 $\sigma$ for
certainty, it indicates a potential excess that deserves further investigation
in future analyses.

a re-examination of the Earth through Cosmic Rays (ETCR) upper limit with a

nonequilibrium thermodynamics to study expansion/contraction processes. Here,
the numbers of initial and final microstates are different so they cannot be
connected by unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This commonly happens when the
phase space volume changes, and has not been studied so far using Hamiltonian
trajectories that can be inverted to yield an identity mapping between initial
and final microstates as the parameter in the Hamiltonian is changed. We
propose a trick to overcome this hurdle with a focus on free expansion in an
isolated system, where the concept of dissipated work is not clear. The trick
is shown to be thermodynamically consistent and can be extremely useful in
simulation. We justify that it is the thermodynamic average of the internal
microwork done by a microstate that is dissipated; this microwork is different
from the exchange microwork with the vacuum, which vanishes. We also establish
that the microwork is nonnegative for free expansion, which is remarkable,
since its sign is not fixed in a general process.
  We have developed a nonequilibrium thermodynamic formalism to study
internal microwork for arbitrary processes, which can be used as a useful
check on other scenarios, including free expansion. The formalism can also be
used to study the microwork between two nonequilibrium steady states and
establish that it is zero, which is expected. We have also established that
the microwork between two equilibrium states at different volumes is
nonnegative, which is remarkable, because of the contraction (expansion) of the
phase space volume from its maximum equilibrium value. This result is expected
to have implications to the issues related to the volume in thermodynamics.
Further, we have derived an expression for the average internal microwork in
terms of the Helmholtz free energy difference between the initial and final
equilibrium states. We have also shown that the average internal microwork
computed by thermodynamic averaging is equal to the microwork done by a
representative trajectory (called microwork averaged trajectory) in phase space
whether or not thermodynamic conditions are satisfied by the system. This
result is remarkable and has been successfully checked for several processes.
It is expected to be useful in simulation to study such complex processes where
thermodynamic conditions are not satisfied.

trained using standard methods, such as inducing points. This enables graph
Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be employed in mini-batch and non-conjugate
settings, thereby making them more accessible to practitioners and easier to
deploy within larger learning frameworks.

classification benchmark and a set of continuous control tasks, wherein their

operation of the urban transportation system and the functionality of urban

inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourcing data from massive
urban travelers (e.g., Google Map). These data have the drawbacks of high

penetration. This study investigates an innovative approach of drive-by
sensing, which leverages large-scale ridesourcing vehicles (RVs) to monitor and
infer the states of urban road networks. With RV traversing over road networks,
we examine the RV fleet sensing performance based on the unique number of road
segments explicitly visited, the sensing reliability as a result of repeated
visits, and the information that can be implicitly inferred given explicit data
and road network topology. We propose an optimal rerouting model to
simultaneously maximize the sensing coverage and sensing reliability, which can
be efficiently solved using a heuristic algorithm to guide the cruising
trajectory of unoccupied RVs sequentially. To validate the effectiveness of the
proposed model, comprehensive experiments and sensitivity analyses are
performed using real-world RV data of more than 20,000 vehicles in New York
City (NYC). Our approach is shown to cover up to 75.5% of all road segments,
which leads to an implicit coverage of 97.2%. More importantly, the optimal
rerouting sequence improves the detection of traffic incidents (e.g., lane
closure) by 27.3%-41.8%, which outperforms traditional camera-based methods
utilizing open-source data (Street Advisor). While our analysis focuses on
Ridesourcing vehicles, the framework is extendable to all circulating vehicles
equipped with onboard sensors whenever their trajectories are available.

the same number of function evaluations. For example, a finite difference
method of order $p$ requires the evaluation of $f$ at $p$ points to compute
approximation to $y(t_{2})$, whereas a SGLM of order $p$ requires only one
evaluation of $f$ to compute approximation to $y(t_{2})$.

relationship? Our answer is that
  \[ imperative\ algorithms\ =\ proofs\ with\ cuts \]
  This observation leads to a generalization to pseudocodes which we call {\it
logical pseudocodes}. It is similar to natural deduction proof of computability
logic\cite{Jap03,Jap08}. Each statement in it corresponds to a proof step in
natural deduction. Therefore, the merit over pseudocode is that each statement
is guaranteed to be correct and safe with respect to the initial
specifications. It can also be seen as an extension to computability logic web
(\colw) with forward reasoning capability.
  We show how various problems including halting problem can be solved using
logical pseudocodes/algorithms. The advantage over standard pseudocodes is
that the solutions are correct and safe with respect to initial specifications
without any restriction on the values of inputs.
  The concept of logical pseudocodes can also be applied to other logics such
as linear logic and resource-sensitive logic. It can also be used to evaluate
the expressiveness of a logic by developing algorithms (proofs) for some
universal computation problems within that logic.
  We also show how algorithmic ideas developed in logical pseudocodes can be
refined to small-sized proofs in natural deduction proof system of \colw, which
can be interesting to logicians.
  All of the examples given in this paper are simple enough to be understood
without prior knowledge of computability logic and its web framework. Their
design also follows some simple guidelines which should be applicable to
other problems as well.
  The main idea used in constructing algorithms (proofs) is to simply and
clearly apply the rules of the logic underlying the logical pseudocode, without
any attempt to mimic the standard pseudocode for the problem on the underlying
computational model (Turing machine, register machine, etc). Such an
underlying computational model is simply a tool providing guarantees on the
availability of resources needed by the algorithm. With a logic-based
approach, one can develop algorithms using the logic's resources (e.g., atomic
propositions in \colw) in a straightforward way, without having to worry about
the implementation details.

robotics. We present a study on using learning-based methods for solving this
problem online from a single RGB image, whilst training our models with
entirely synthetic data. We study three main approaches: one direct regression
model that directly predicts the extrinsic matrix from an image, one sparse
correspondence model that regresses 2D keypoints and then uses PnP, and one
dense correspondence model that uses regressed depth and segmentation maps to
enable ICP pose estimation. In our experiments, we benchmark these methods
against each other and against well-established classical methods, to find the
surprising result that direct regression outperforms other approaches, and we
perform noise-sensitivity analysis to gain further insights into these results.
We conclude that with sufficient data and architecture tuning, direct
regression models can achieve superior performance compared to alternative
methods while being much simpler to implement.

well-maintained benchmark suite that can be easily extended to try out other
variants. Finally, we argue that future work should focus on enabling these
learning-based methods to work well on real images, and we provide a
method-dependent guide to do so.

degraded measurements. Such problems arise in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI),
computed tomography, deblurring, superresolution, inpainting, and other
applications. It is often the case that many image hypotheses are consistent
with both the measurements and prior information, and so the goal is not to
recover a single "best" hypothesis but rather to explore the space of probable
hypotheses, i.e., to sample from the posterior distribution. In this work, we
propose a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN that can generate dozens of
high-quality posterior samples per second. Using quantitative evaluation
metrics like conditional Fr\'{e}chet inception distance, we demonstrate that
our method produces state-of-the-art posterior samples in both multicoil MRI
and inpainting applications.
  We also introduce a novel visualization technique that allows the user to
recover detailed information about individual samples and the underlying
posterior distribution. While our method produces inferior synthetic images
when compared to prior works, it excels in real-image applications where
high-quality samples are often tolerably inferior to render a sense of
plausibility, coupled with the ability to generate high volumes of content, to
produce a satisfactory solution.
  Having high-quality posterior sampling capability enables us to perform
conditional generation of multiple images at varying encoding grids, render
details that are missing in the input image, and generate images with specific
traits. We show that our method can generate MRI images that better preserve
details and have less artifacts compared to prior works. Furthermore, we show
that our method can generate inpainted images that are perceptually smoother
and have fewer artifacts.
  Finally, we propose a post-processing technique called posterior refinement,
which improves the visual quality of existing sampling methods without the need
for a new conditional Wasserstein GAN training. Refined samples exhibit
remarkable visual improvements with respect to conventional evaluation
metrics.

that can utilize a pre-trained conditional Wasserstein GAN as a component. We

parabolas in planar polynomial systems. We provide the conditions for the
invariance of linear subspaces in fractional order systems. Further, we provide

  From the control perspective, if a trajectory is initially confined to an
invariant manifold, it will stay on it forever, thus providing a convenient
means of satisfying control objectives. Importing this concept to dynamical
systems with coexisting stable and unstable regions, our purpose is to design
control systems that place the initial condition of the system on an invariant
manifold so that the trajectory follows a stable invariant manifold pointing
towards the stable equilibrium while keeping a desired distance. Our approach
provides a means of exploiting the invariant manifold structure of the system
without explicitly solving the ordinary differential equations defining the
manifold, thus offering a beneficial simplification in the design. We illustrate
the effectiveness of the proposed approach in a nonlinear mass-damper-spring
system, a cargo delivery quadrotor system, and an inverted pendulum on a
carriage system.

dubbed "reference trajectory with invariant manifold assistance" (RITIAM). We
employ a nonlinear invariance enrichment controller (IIC) to force the ASV
trajectory to approach and stay near a reference trajectory while traveling
towards a desired invariant manifold that assists the nearness. We consider the
case when the reference trajectory is known exactly and when it is unknown but
estimatable. In the former case, we use the IIC to modify the finite-time
Lagrangian controller (FLC) by adding an invariant manifold assistance component
to reap the benefits of invariant manifolds. In the latter case, we modify the
nonlinear robust reproduction controller (NRRC) by adding an invariant manifold
assistance component to benefit from the accuracy of the estimation and the
precision of the NRRC. We experimentally verify the effectiveness of our
control architecture in both cases.

achieving extremely high data rates in next-generation wireless networks. While
the THz communication is conventionally envisioned for short-range wireless
applications due to the high atmospheric absorption at THz frequencies,
multi-hop directional transmissions can be enabled to extend the communication
range. However, to realize multi-hop THz communications, conventional beam
training schemes, such as exhaustive search or hierarchical methods with a
fixed number of training levels, can lead to a very large time overhead. To
address this challenge, in this paper, a novel hierarchical beam training
scheme with dynamic training levels is proposed to optimize the performance of
multi-hop THz links. In fact, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize
the overall spectral efficiency of the multi-hop THz link by dynamically and
jointly selecting the number of beam training levels across all the constituent
single-hop links. To solve this problem in presence of unknown channel state
information, noise, and path loss, a new reinforcement learning solution based
on the multi-armed bandit (MAB) is developed. Simulation results show the fast
convergence of the proposed scheme in presence of random channels and noise.
The results also show that the proposed scheme can yield up to 75% performance
gain, in terms of spectral efficiency, compared to the conventional
hierarchical beam training with a fixed number of training levels.

scattering screens, most of
unknown origin. Scintillation studies of pulsars provides a sensitive tool for
resolving these scattering screens and a means of measuring their properties.
In this paper, we report our analysis of 34 years of Arecibo observations of
PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens
located along the line of sight to the pulsar. We have identified six
individual scattering screens that are responsible for the observed
scintillation arcs, which persist for decades. Using the assumption that the
scattering screens have not changed significantly in this time, we have modeled
the variations in arc curvature throughout the Earth's orbit and extracted
information about the placement, orientation, and velocity of five of the six
screens, with the highest-precision distance measurement placing a screen at
just $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from the Earth. We associate the more distant of
these screens with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble.
  We also report evidence for the formation and evolution of a new scattering
screen located very close to the Earth, originating from plasma ejected from
Machholz meteorite debris left in Earth's atmosphere. The formation process
occurred within $\lesssim$2 months of 2014. The density of this screen has
increased by a factor of $\approx$10 since its formation, with the increase
occurring rapidly ($\lesssim$1 year). The new screen has a substantial
orientation ($\approx$70$^{\circ}$) from the Earth's velocity vector, and its
location has evolved from within the Earth's magnetosphere to in the
interplanetary medium, where it continues to be observed. Evolution of this
screen and possibly other planetary screens is ideal for statistical study
using the full population of pulsars.
  We lastly note that even with the powerful tool that pulsar scintillation
provides for resolving the interstellar medium, there remain scattering screens
of unascertained origin. And it is clear that multiple other screens are
located along the lines of sight to other pulsars that have not yet been
resolved.

long- and short-term dependencies of quasi-periodic signals such as speech. The
performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The
experimental results show the effectiveness of the PDCNNs for unseen auxiliary
$F_{0}$ features and the effectiveness of the cascaded structure for speech
generation.

  Sound source localization (LS) from video has recently attracted the attention
of the research community. Unlike vision keypoint localization, the novel
application of deep learning to sound source localization is still in its
infancy and very few datasets exist. A novel challenge posed by the lack of
existing large-scale datasets is the novel environment bias: deep networks are
known to capture biases towards the population they are trained on, and that
means that the models trained on a small set of environments will underperform
on new, unseen settings. Our key technical contribution is to show that, by
training the network to explicitly discriminate challenging image fragments,
even for images that do contain the object emitting the sound, we can
significantly bootstrap localization performance across novel domains. We do
so elegantly by introducing a mechanism to mine hard samples and add them to a
contrastive learning formulation automatically. Both quantitative and
qualitative experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art
performance on the recently-introduced VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) dataset, which
contains 5K videos spanning over 200 categories and is 20 times larger than
existing similar ones.

attention recently. Most GCNs learn the node representations in Euclidean
geometry, but that could have a high distortion in the case of embedding graphs
with scale-free or hierarchical structure. Recently, some GCNs are proposed to
deal with this problem in non-Euclidean geometry, e.g., hyperbolic geometry.
Although hyperbolic GCNs achieve promising performance, existing hyperbolic
graph operations actually cannot rigorously follow the hyperbolic geometry,
which may limit the ability of hyperbolic geometry and thus hurt the
performance of hyperbolic GCNs. In this paper, we propose a novel hyperbolic
GCN named Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which rigorously
guarantees the learned node features follow the hyperbolic geometry.
Specifically, we rebuild the graph operations of hyperbolic GCNs with
Lorentzian version, e.g., the feature transformation and non-linear activation.
Also, an elegant neighborhood aggregation method is designed based on the
centroid of Lorentzian distance. Moreover, we prove that the proposed
transformation and aggregation are equivalent in hyperbolic feature space.
Extensive experiments on six datasets show that LGCN performs better than the
state-of-the-art methods. LGCN has lower distortion and could learn more
robust node representations, thus improves the performance of hyperbolic GCNs.
LGCN has a lower training complexity and can be trained with a smaller mini-batch
size compared to the tube GCN. LGCN is proved to be more efficient in
learning the graph structure without increasing the parameter size.

natural images, their application to the medical domain, however, is still in
its infancy. Working with the CheXpert data set, we show that StyleGAN can be
trained to generate realistic chest X-rays. Inspired by the Cyclic Reverse

reconstructions of real ones. Employing a guided manipulation of latent codes,
we confer the medical condition of cardiomegaly (CardioMega) onto both real and
generated X-rays. This work was presented in the Medical Imaging

and analysis of multidimensional
vectorial data. ViDaExpert is able to work with data tables of "object-feature"
type that might contain numerical feature values as well as textual labels for
rows (objects) and columns (features). ViDaExpert implements several
statistical methods such as standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis
(PCA) and the method of elastic maps (non-linear version of PCA), Linear
Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, a
variant of decision tree construction algorithm. Equipped with several
user-friendly dialogs for configuring data point representations (size, shape,
color) and fast 3D viewer, ViDaExpert is a handy tool allowing to construct an
interactive 3D-scene representing a table of data in multidimensional space and
perform its quick and insightfull statistical analysis, from basic to advanced
methods.
  ViDaExpert is written in C++ using the OpenGL library for the purpose of
fast 3D visualization. The ATLAS LAPACK and BLAS libraries are used to speed
up the computational operations. The use of the Standard Template Library (STL)
made the development of new stats methods easier and more robust. ViDaExpert
works under Microsoft Windows operating system, at least Windows XP.
  ViDaExpert source code is delivered. If you are interested in modifying the
code or adding your own algorithms, please contact me at
kreshd@gmail.com, I'd gladly welcome your contribution and would be happy to
assist you with the integration of your new feature/statistic method.
  ViDaExpert was developed in the course of my Ph.D. research at the Biodynamic
Dancing Research Project, www.dancingphd.com. It was used internally for the
analysis of the movement data acquired using the optical motion capture system.
If you are working with movement data, please consider using ViDaExpert to
quickly and effectively visualize and analyze them. It might also be useful
for other fields where high-dimensional data is present.
  ViDaExpert comes with a small set of sample data tables and a tutorial help
manual. You are welcome to send me your feedback, suggestions and reports on
ViDaExpert performance on your data.

potentials over general
2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
monomial approximation of a function over a mesh element, which is often
regarded as an ill-conditioned problem, since it involves the solution of a
Vandermonde linear system. In fact, it has long been observed that, when the
function is sufficiently smooth, and when a backward stable linear system
solver is used, the resulting monomial expansion can approximate the function
uniformly to high accuracy. We rigorously formalize this observation in this
paper. The performance of our algorithm is illustrated through several
numerical experiments.
  We believe that our algorithm has the potential to significantly improve the
efficiency of volume integral equation methods in electromagnetics and
acoustics. As a first step towards this, we have implemented our algorithm into
a high-performance FMM-based volume integral equation solver (called
$fi$ctitious Domain Integrated Equation Solver, or FIDES) and solved several
typical problems in electromagnetics. The benefits of FIDES are illustrated
through several numerical examples, where we compare the time-instruction
instruction count of FIDES with that of the state-of-the-art HPMMIDIEs solver.
FIDES is written in C++ using the Armadillo and FMMTL libraries, and is
available under the terms of the GPL license. The FMMTL library is a
high-performance implementation of the classic FMM algorithm for evaluating
Coulomb and linear rational potentials between general domains. It is written by
R. Cooley and J. Wilcox, and is available under the terms of the GPL license.
